findings.problem: Cites "the precedent set at C05, C09 and C10, where the verdict marks a list running two proofs that cancel". On a page whose product is provenance, a mis-cited internal precedent is the worst available kind of slip, and it is checkable in one click.

findings.problem: "the 4/3 factor is the standard-atmosphere case, a duct is a larger k, and a sub-refractive layer is a smaller one." Sub-refraction is correctly a smaller k, but a duct is not "a larger k": in the standard treatment k = 1/(1 + a dn/dh), superrefraction is k > 4/3, and ducting begins at dN/dh = -157 N/km, exactly where k passes through infinity (the ray follows the Earth's curvature) and then goes negative. That is the point where the effective-earth-radius model degenerates and engineering practice switches to modified refractivity and parabolic-equation solvers. An RF engineer will spot this in the one paragraph the entry offers as "the honest qualification" — and the correct version is STRONGER for us, because modified refractivity is M = N + 0.157h and 0.157 per metre is 10^6/R: the standard ducting formalism is an earth-flattening transformation whose flattening term is proportional to 1/R, which is precisely the §5 thesis.
findings.fix: Replace with: superrefraction is a larger k; a duct is the limit at which the effective-radius model itself breaks, and the standard treatment beyond it is modified refractivity M = N + 0.157h — an earth-flattening transformation whose 0.157 per metre is 10^6/R. Then the ducting concession lands on the same 1/R structure as the rest of the entry.

findings.problem: Three numbers are chained as one computation and they come from two incompatible models. The 61.0° and the 7.3 m across-track follow from Snell with c 1% high (I reproduce 61.02° and 7.24 m). The "about 1.0 m of vertical error" does not follow from that geometry: applying the same 1.02° bend at 100 m gives roughly 4 m, and holding travel time with c 1% high gives about 2.2 m. 1.0 m is 1% of depth — the range-scaling error for a uniform bias with no bending at all. The passage is explicitly labelled "recomputed here", so a hydrographer who reproduces it gets a different number, and the headline "eats 72% of the entire allowance" inherits the mismatch. Note the direction: our figure UNDERSTATES, so the argument survives — this is a coherence defect, not a wrong conclusion.
findings.fix: Attribute each number to its mechanism: a 1% bias in the mean sound speed puts about 1.0 m into a 100 m sounding through the range scaling alone, and the 1° of ray bending it implies at a 60° outer beam moves the sounding about 7 m across-track and adds several times that vertical error at the swath edge — against an Order 1a allowance of 1.39 m.

findings.field: refutation §3, TZDS paragraph (scripts/_b10_B11.py:282) and the Fiedler source label (scripts/_b10_B11.py:539-543)
findings.problem: Total zero-Doppler steering is described as "a yaw manoeuvre" and the label calls it "the yaw-steering law developed for TerraSAR-X". The cited paper's own abstract opens: "This letter presents a new method, called total Zero Doppler steering, to perform YAW AND PITCH steering for spaceborne SAR systems", and Zhao & Wei — the other source we cite — describe TZDS as "exploiting an additional pitch steering". Yaw-only steering is the earlier, weaker method; the added pitch term is the cited paper's entire contribution. The load-bearing point (the spacecraft steers attitude against the Earth's rotation, at an angle derived from omega-Earth) is untouched.
findings.fix: "a continuous yaw-and-pitch steering law", and in the label "the yaw-and-pitch steering law developed for TerraSAR-X". The yaw term is the one derived from the Earth's rotation rate; the pitch term absorbs the orbit eccentricity, which is what Zhao & Wei's quoted sentence names alongside it.

findings.problem: "Airborne early warning aircraft carry a radar up a tower fifty times higher than any mast can be built." The tallest masts ever built are about 630-646 m, so an AEW aircraft at the 10 km the entry itself uses two paragraphs earlier is about fifteen times higher, not fifty. The figure only works against a 200 m tower, which is not "any mast that can be built". It sits three sentences from a run of exact recomputed numbers, which is where a loose figure costs the most.

The abstract (WHOI 1912/2044, dated 1942-07-25, verified) continues "..., especially on shallow targets." The omission does not change the sense — the dropped clause is an intensifier, not a qualifier — but it presents a truncated sentence as a complete one, in an entry that is otherwise scrupulous about quoting hedges whole.

findings.problem: Both published fields state that item 252's Moon-tide mismatch is something "the canon's own carriers deny in the sentence next to the one it took" / that "Winship's sentence denies". The located texts say the reverse. On p. 130 of Zetetic Cosmogony — the page immediately before the sentence we quote, and reprinted as "(130-131)" by the Christian Flat Earth Ministry page we cite — Winship writes in his own voice: "But the tides are not uniform. At Port Natal the rise and fall is about six feet, while at Beira, about 600 miles up the coast, the rise and fall is 26 feet. This effectually settles the matter that the moon has no influence on the tides." On p. 131 he prints Melville approvingly: "The Newtonian theory of the Tides does not hold good at Tahiti". And Dubay's proof 118, which the entry's own docstring note 2 records, says flatly "the Earth's tides vary greatly and do not follow the Moon". Our own refutation §5 (line 262) says Winship "treated it as decisive" — so the entry asserts and denies the same thing about the same source. This is the hedge rule inverted: we quoted the concession and stopped where the flat statement sits.
findings.fix: Replace the item-252 paragraph in compression.note with the honest result: "Item 252, “Tidal bores moon visual timing”: this one does not drift on the mismatch. Winship asserts it flatly on p. 130 — “the tides are not uniform…This effectually settles the matter that the moon has no influence on the tides” — prints Melville’s Tahiti observation on p. 131 as proof of it, and Dubay’s proof 118 carries it forward as “the Earth’s tides vary greatly and do not follow the Moon”. What the list drops is the concession Winship attaches on the next page, that the Moon is nonetheless “the TIMEKEEPER for the tides” whose phase “tells what kind of a tide may be expected”, and Scott’s “of this we cannot now be sure”. That is hedge_dropped, not a reversal. Bores are a separate matter: no bore passage is located in any of the tide texts searched for this entry." Amend the gloss sentence at line 206 to match: strike "that Winship's sentence denies" and write instead that Winship asserts the mismatch and concedes the timekeeping in the same two pages.

findings.problem: The authors are wrong. Crossref for the DOI in our own URL (10.1029/2018JC014695) returns Peng, Hill, Meltzner and Switzer — JGR Oceans 124:736-749 (2019). findings.fix: Body: "Peng and colleagues examined tide-gauge records worldwide and found that cycle changes high water levels by up to 30 cm." Source label: "Peng, Hill, Meltzner & Switzer, \"Tide Gauge Records Show That the 18.61-Year Nodal Tidal Cycle Can Change High Water Levels by up to 30 cm\", JGR Oceans 124:736-749 (2019)".

findings.field: compression (list_phrasing / source_wording / drift_type / note headline, lines 363-380)
findings.problem: The block's headline finding — "A row its own author scored as non-discriminating arrives on the list as item 245" — depends on identifying item 245, "Tidal resonance geocentric.", with the p. 794 table row, and that identification is asserted with no evidence and one live competitor. The p. 794 cell contains no resonance content of any kind: I searched the item's OCR and "resonan*" occurs on printed pages 633, 634, 809, 855, 864, 872, 875, 876, 888, 906, 965 and 1101 — and not on 794. findings.fix: Add to the first paragraph of compression.note, after the p. 820 sentence: "The identification is ours and it is an inference: the row is the only place in the located tide passages where the geocentric literature answers a tidal argument, but the cell says nothing about resonance, and the book's one extended resonance passage — Hoyle on the atmosphere at printed pp. 633–634 — is about tidal braking of rotation and is treated in the length-of-day cluster. If a reader rejects the identification, the consequence is that no source was located for item 245 either, which is a finding of the same weight."

findings.problem: The section is headed "The proposed alternatives, answered on their own hedged terms" and then answers Rowbotham past his hedge. Two problems. First, the prediction attributed to him — "high water simultaneous along the coasts" — is not what he wrote; his stated consequence is "The simultaneous ebb and flow upon meridians 180 degrees apart", which standard theory also delivers. Second, every datum deployed against it falls inside the qualifier our own block quote reproduces four paragraphs earlier: "Whatever peculiarities are observable they may be traced to the reaction of channels, bays, headlands, and other local causes." Holyhaven against London Bridge is an estuary, the St Lawrence and Amazon are rivers — the exact class he scoped out. A defender who has read our own passage quote wins this paragraph.
findings.fix: Rewrite the opening of that paragraph to quote the hedge and answer it: "Rowbotham's stated consequence is narrower than it looks — ‘the simultaneous ebb and flow upon meridians 180° apart’ — and he pre-empts local disagreement by tracing ‘whatever peculiarities are observable’ to ‘channels, bays, headlands, and other local causes’. Take the escape at face value and it costs him the model's only quantitative content: once channel reaction can supply any phase at any place, the floating plane predicts nothing about when high water arrives anywhere, and the prediction it does make in its own voice — a period fixed by the plate's size, ‘once only in about twelve hours’ — is the one that fails, because the period is 12 h 25 min and tracks the Moon." Then keep the Peacock data as illustration of a progressive wave rather than as the refutation. Note that the verdict_challenge reasoning (line 426-429) leans on the same Peacock leg and should be re-worded with it.

findings.field: passage.gloss, "The other strand, and its one sentence" (line 210)
findings.problem: "The geocentric literature reaches this topic once." is an unscoped claim about an entire corpus drawn from one book, which is the project's dominant confirmed failure mode, and the regex in tests/test_provenance.py does not match this phrasing — a live instance of "writers have learned the regex, not the rule". It is also loose about the one book it did search: "tide"/"tidal" occurs on roughly twenty-two printed pages of the 2006 PDF, and pp. 631-635 discuss tides at length (Hoyle, atmospheric tides, tidal braking).

In Galileo Was Wrong (2006 PDF, 1,160 pp.), where the strings “tide” and “tidal” occur on some two dozen printed pages — mostly tidal braking of rotation at pp. 631–635 and the historical Galileo material at pp. 1026–1029 — ch. 12, printed p. 794 carries the one sentence that offers a mechanism."

findings.problem: "Set the Earth's rotation to zero and there is no Coriolis deflection, no Kelvin wave, and no amphidromic point", and §8's "one requires the Earth to turn", are stated flatly against a cluster one of whose two strands is geocentric — and the geocentric literature's standard answer to every Coriolis argument is that a universe rotating about a fixed Earth supplies the same inertial effects by frame dragging. The entry cites Bennett, lists A13 and A15 in `related`, and the project already has cluster records on Mach's principle and frame dragging, so the move is one the entry knows about and does not meet. The trailing "the cotidal charts the item points at would be blank" is separately overstated: a non-rotating ocean still has tides and cotidal lines, it has nodal lines rather than rotary amphidromes.
findings.fix: End the §2 paragraph: "— the cotidal charts would show nodal lines rather than the rotary systems the item points at. The geocentric reply is that a universe turning about a fixed Earth supplies the same inertial forces by frame dragging; that answer is taken up at ARG-A13, and note what it costs here: it concedes that the handedness of every amphidrome is set by rotation, and argues only about which body is turning. The flat-earth strand of this cluster, which has no rotation of any kind, has no version of that reply available." Then soften §8 to "one is made by rotation, on any account of which body is doing the rotating".

findings.problem: "No version of tidal theory has ever claimed the Moon lifts water against terrestrial gravity" is an unscoped absolute about a whole literature, and it is the weakest sentence in the entry because the tradition is demonstrably answering expositions that said just that. Winship's p. 130 — the page next to the one we quote — reproduces "Her attraction (the moon's) draws up the yielding waters of the ocean in a vast wave" and Ball's claim that the Moon attracts the solid body of the Earth. Our own steelman concedes the two-bulge cartoon was and is taught. Physically, too, the vertical component of the tide-raising force at the sublunar point is directed upward; the correct point is that it is 10^-7 of gravity and that the work is done horizontally, not that nobody ever spoke of lifting.
findings.fix: "The mass argument answers the popular exposition rather than the theory. Rowbotham and Winship were reading sentences like the one Winship reprints on p. 130 — ‘her attraction draws up the yielding waters of the ocean in a vast wave’ — and against that picture the objection has force. It has none against tidal theory proper, in which the tide-raising acceleration is the residual left when the Moon's pull on the ocean is compared with its pull on the Earth's centre: about one ten-millionth of surface gravity, with a vertical component too small to lift anything and a horizontal component that drags water sideways over ocean-basin distances."

findings.problem: The advocate rates the curve-fitting charge as the move that earns the 4 and the preemptive requires the body to concede it "in its own voice" — "harmonic prediction IS empirical, Kelvin's machine did work without a theory of the ocean, and nothing in section 6 should be allowed to imply otherwise". No such concession exists in the published fields. "Kelvin" appears in the body only as "Kelvin wave" in §2; the §8 concession list omits the point entirely; and the steelman's "Harmonic analysis of a real record returns power at those lines and, to first order, nowhere else" is the sentence that invites the objection. Since `advocate` is stripped from the published corpus by build.py, the required change has nowhere to land except the refutation, and it has not landed there.
findings.fix: Add to §6, before "Now take the kernel's own best case": "Concede the obvious first: harmonic tide prediction is empirical, and Kelvin's 1870s brass machine predicted tides beautifully while embodying no theory of the ocean at all. The basis set is what is not fitted. Doodson's six arguments are the Moon's and Sun's longitudes, lunar perigee, the lunar node and perihelion, all fixed by astrometry before a gauge is read — so the expansion is a prediction about which lines will carry power, and any line that carries power and is not among them falsifies it."

findings.problem: The TLDR hardens the one hedged source sentence the entry relies on, in our favour. Galileo Was Wrong Vol. I (verified in the archive.org djvu text, on the page following the printed 855 marker) reads: "Geocentrism's Response: Only light and gases show ether effects; the experiment was incapable of achieving ether detection unless a charged gas is used between the plates." The refutation and the untraceable block both quote the sentence in full, so this is a summary that outruns its own body, in the field with the highest reader impact, committing on our side the exact drift this project publishes as a finding against the list.

Roughly the same length, and it survives being checked.

findings.field: untraceable (final sentence of the Rowbotham paragraph)
findings.problem: "The refutation above answers that argument, at its own strength, in his own numbers" is false twice over. (a) The refutation contains no answer to Rowbotham's reattribution: searching all published fields, "thermal" and "expansion" occur only in the untraceable block, "Noad", "temperature", "5000" and "39.027" occur nowhere in the refutation, and its only uses of "air" are free-air corrections and aircraft.
