findings.field: refutation §3 and sources[21] (Wettzell G ring laser)
findings.problem: "the G instrument at Wettzell tracks the Earth's rotation rate to below one part in 10^9, resolving length-of-day variation and polar motion in agreement with VLBI", cited to Eur. Phys. J. C 82 (2022) — Di Virgilio et al., arXiv:2208.09134. The paper supports the first clause (its title is "Overcoming 1 part in 10^9 of earth angular rotation rate measurement with the G Wettzell data" and the Allan deviation drops below 1e-9 after ~1e4 s). It does not support the second: the full text contains zero occurrences of "VLBI" and no occurrence of "length of day", and polar motion appears only as IERS-published Chandler and annual-wobble terms subtracted from the ring-laser data as corrections — corrections the paper itself calls preliminary "since the absolute orientation of the G structure is not known well enough". So the cited paper treats polar motion as an input, roughly the opposite of the independent-confirmation reading our sentence invites. The claim itself is true and documented elsewhere, which makes this a sourcing failure rather than a physics one.
findings.fix: Split the citation: keep EPJC 82 (2022) for the 1-part-in-10^9 stability, and cite the VLBI comparison to its own source (e.g. "Earth rotation variations observed by VLBI and the Wettzell 'G' ring laser during the CONT17 campaign", Adv. Geosci. 50:9, 2019) — or drop "in agreement with VLBI" and say only that the instrument resolves the Earth's rotation rate to below one part in 10^9 with no moving parts, which is all §3 needs.

findings.field: untraceable ("Why this is not filed as older than the movement")
findings.problem: "Instruments this sensitive did not exist before the movement did: the superconducting gravimeter dates from the 1960s, the Cavendish balance from 1798, the Eötvös torsion balance from the 1890s." The sentence is refuted by its own list — 1798 precedes the movement, which this review dates to Rowbotham 1849 (README: "writing 1849-65") — and by the entry's own refutation §2, which rests on Richer's 1672 clock and Kater's 1818 reversible pendulum, i.e. on instruments of exactly the relevant sensitivity, two centuries early. Since a pendulum-clock argument was mechanically available long before the movement, the stated reason for rejecting the pre_modern origin state is the wrong reason, and it sits in the paragraph justifying one of the three origin states the project treats as central.
findings.fix: Rest the paragraph on the correct ground and delete the instrument-dating sentence: "That state records where an argument came from, and it needs an old text that contains the argument. Precision pendulum work is old enough — Richer 1672, Kater 1818 — but no pre-modern text we searched argues from instrument constancy to a stationary Earth, and the gravimeter and the torsion balance postdate the movement's founding texts. There is nothing in the works listed above to inherit from."

findings.problem: The kernel is over-scoped against the modern experiment it cites. "The modern version keeps the same dependence" and "Cite the null and you have cited an instrument whose sensitivity is a function of ω" are true for the Earth-as-source configuration (the classic ~1.7e-3 g suppression Eötvös used) but not for Schlamminger et al. 2008 as a whole, whose abstract reports accelerations "towards sources at a variety of distances", improving limits "with ranges from 1 m to infinity". A laboratory attractor at 1 m produces a horizontal differential acceleration by construction, with no ω in the channel. A physicist-defender can therefore confine the argument to 1909 and claim the modern null back.
findings.fix: Scope both sentences to the source: "...the channel through which that difference could show up, when the Earth is the attractor — Eötvös's configuration, and the one the item invokes — is the horizontal component of the centrifugal acceleration... Modern balances add laboratory attractor masses, whose signal does not depend on ω; but a null against a 1 m attractor says nothing at all about the Earth's motion, so it is not a null the item can use either."

findings.field: untraceable and compression.note ("the reachable geocentric corpus")
findings.problem: "That is the only torsion-balance null on point anywhere in the reachable geocentric corpus", repeated in compression.note as "the only null on point in the reachable geocentric corpus". This is a uniqueness claim ranging over an unnamed literature, established from six specific works — precisely the construction the standing rule bans ("never write that an absence exists; write that X is not located in the specific text you searched"). "Reachable" gestures at a scope without naming one, and neither field states which corpus was reached.
findings.fix: Name the searched set in both fields: "That is the only torsion-balance null on point in the six works searched above — both volumes of Galileo Was Wrong, Rowbotham 1865, Carpenter 1885, Dubay's 200 Proofs and Hendrie 2016 — and the book declines to bank it."

findings.field: untraceable ("The Victorian trunk of the tradition", final sentence)
findings.problem: "Both pendulum discussions are about Foucault precession, which this review scores at ARG-A06" is contradicted by the next paragraph of the same block, which is built on Rowbotham's seconds-pendulum/latitude passage. In Gutenberg #69892, 14 of the 78 lines containing "pendulum" fall in Section I (the equator-to-pole passage), and 64 in the Foucault material of Section 12. Carpenter's proof 73 is Foucault; Rowbotham's discussion is not exclusively so, and the entry's own best find depends on that.
findings.fix: "Carpenter's discussion is Foucault precession, which this review scores at ARG-A06. Rowbotham's divides: 64 of his 78 hits fall in the Foucault section, and 14 in the Section I passage discussed next — which is where this search stopped being routine."

findings.problem: "the pendulum had to be made 1.25 lignes — 2.256 mm — shorter than at Paris" is a wrong conversion. The Paris ligne is 1/12 pouce = 2.2558 mm, so 1.25 lignes is 2.82 mm; 2.256 mm is one ligne. The cited Wikipedia article carries the same slip, so it was inherited rather than invented — but it is published in our voice, in a section whose force comes from arithmetic, and it is checkable in one line by anyone who wants to knock the page down.
findings.fix: Write "1.25 lignes (about 2.8 mm)" in both the refutation and the source label, and either drop the parenthetical or footnote the ligne (2.2558 mm) so the conversion is auditable.

findings.problem: The label credits that article with "the burnt thread and the Charron ring". The burnt thread is there verbatim, as are "requires care to set up because imprecise construction can cause additional veering which masks the terrestrial effect" and the perturbation result that "geometrical imperfection of the system or elasticity of the support wire may cause a beat between two horizontal modes of oscillation". "Charron" does not occur anywhere in the article (checked against the raw wikitext, 0 hits), so the refutation's Charron-ring sentence in §3 is currently unsourced. The device is real; the citation is simply the wrong one.
findings.fix: Drop "and the Charron ring" from the label and give the ring its own citation, or delete the half-sentence "and why a Charron ring is fitted to bleed off the ellipticity" — §3 loses nothing, since the elliptical-precession point is already carried by the wire-elasticity sentence the article does support.

findings.field: untraceable ("The Victorian trunk" and "The modern compilers")
findings.problem: Two search-scoping claims are each off by one hit, and both are the kind of number a hostile reader re-runs. Carpenter's seven "pendulum" hits are described as "all of them proof 73 and the index line"; the seventh is a metaphor in the closing essay ("swayed back again like a gigantic pendulum"). Dubay's nine are described as "all inside proof 140"; the ninth is in proof 141 ("just like Foucault's Pendulums spinning either which way"). The counts themselves (7 and 9) are exactly right, and neither correction changes the finding.
findings.fix: "...seven for 'pendulum' — five in proof 73, one in the index, one a metaphor in the closing essay" and "...nine hits for 'pendulum', eight of them inside proof 140 and the ninth a back-reference in proof 141".

findings.problem: "He writes that 'a pendulum vibrates more rapidly in the northern region than at the equator'" quotes words that are verbatim in Gutenberg #69892 but that sit inside a reported opposing premise: "It has been thought that because a pendulum vibrates more rapidly in the northern region than at the equator, the Earth is thereby proved to be a globe". A defender will say we quoted Rowbotham asserting his opponents' claim. Our characterisation still holds — he concedes the variation outright further down ("Many philosophers have ascribed the alterations in the oscillations of a pendulum to the diminished temperature"; "the variations in the rate of a pendulum as it is carried from the equator towards the north are sufficiently explained") — but the strongest quote is not the one we used.
findings.fix: Swap the quotation for the concession: "He treats the variation as established — the alterations 'in the rate of a pendulum as it is carried from the equator towards the north', which he says are 'sufficiently explained' by temperature and air — and prints the figures."

findings.field: passage.gloss / refutation / compression.source_wording / compression.note / sources[2] / docstring §3, §10
findings.problem: Six of the eight page citations to Galileo Was Wrong Vol. I are one page low against the printed page numbers in the scan the entry names (archive.org item GallileoWasWrong). Verified by mapping the item's hOCR page index to its page-number table and confirmed on the page images themselves: Bennett's ch. 12 'Technical and Summary Analysis of Geocentric Cosmology' opens on printed p. 710, not 709 (page image of leaf 722 shows the chapter title above the footer '710'), and the 'Centrifugal forces cause the water and air near the equator to rise ... the polar flattening and equatorial bulge. This also explains why the acceleration of gravity is less at the equator' sentence is on that page; the 'Claims and Responses / Response: All the various effects noted above depend on the assumption...' text is on p. 711, not 710. Likewise Russell's 'the flattening of the Earth at the poles, and the fact that bodies are heavier there than at the equator' is on p. 49, not 48 (page image of leaf 61 shows footer '49'); Mach quoted in full with 'our law of inertia is wrongly expressed. I prefer the second way' is at ch. 7, p. 460, not 459; the clipped Mach quote ('...and so on...') is on p. 204, not 203 — the same page as the 'not that a rotation of the Earth is the force' sentence the entry cites correctly as p. 204; the WGS84 1/298.257223563 is in Appendix 7 at p. 1028, not 1027; and the satellite-photograph parenthesis in ch. 11 (Hildegardian Geocentrism, confirmed) is at p. 699, not 698. Only ch. 4 p. 204 and ch. 5 p. 239 n. 492 are right (the Einstein footnote is exactly n. 492 on p. 239, and it does cite Annalen der Physik 35, 903). The docstring asserts these 'are the printed numbers in the Vol. I OCR (item GallileoWasWrong)'; they are not. On a page whose product is provenance, and against an in-copyright source a hostile reader will check, a citation that lands on the wrong page is the most expensive kind of error available.
findings.fix: Renumber throughout: 709→710, 710→711, 48→49, 459→460, 203→204, 1027→1028, 698→699. Keep 204 and 239. Then change the docstring's provenance note to say the printed numbers were read from the page images of the named scan (leaves 722, 723, 61, 472, 216, 1040, 711), rather than 'not checked against a print copy', since the scan's own footers are now the evidence.

findings.problem: The TLDR says 'The thermal-expansion coefficient he quotes on the same page is about eight times too small to account for what he is explaining.' The body says the opposite, in as many words: 'The coefficient is not the problem. 1/150,000 per °F is 6.7 × 10⁻⁶/°F, against a modern figure for steel of 11.7 × 10⁻⁶/°C = 6.5 × 10⁻⁶/°F. He quoted a good number and did not multiply it out.' What is eight times too small is the effect — coefficient times his own 84.2 °F range, 0.056% against the 0.436% he has to explain. This is the sweep's recurring failure #2/#6 (TLDR written from memory of the argument), and it hands a defender a free rebuttal from our own text: the entry's centrepiece is that Rowbotham's number was good and his arithmetic absent, and the summary line contradicts it.
findings.fix: Rewrite the clause as: 'and the thermal expansion he offers as the cause — his own good coefficient times his own 84.2 °F equator-to-pole range — comes out about eight times too small to produce it.'

findings.field: passage.gloss (bolded sentence: 'Both books grant the phenomena. Neither of them asserts items 180 or 257.')
findings.problem: An unscoped absence claim about the entire contents of two books, made from the passages read — the dominant confirmed failure across both prior sweeps, and it evades the ratcheting lint only because 'neither of them asserts' is not one of the regex's shapes ('writers have learned the regex, not the rule'). Worse, the entry itself prints two counter-instances from the same volume within the next two paragraphs. At printed p. 699 the book says satellite photographs 'do not show an equatorial bulge'; at p. 711, restating Barbour and Bertotti, it says 'An object at the center of the hollow sphere will not be affected by the inertial forces. The space around the Earth will exhibit the inertial effects of the distant sphere, but not the Earth itself, if it is centrally located' — which is a source statement that no centrifugal effect acts on the Earth, i.e. very close to item 180. The affirmations at pp. 710, 204 and 49 are real and the 'reversed' drift verdict survives on them, but the flat 'neither of them asserts' does not, and a defender who reads section 5 of our own refutation can say so.
findings.fix: Replace with a scoped and honest version: 'No assertion of items 180 or 257 was located in the passages of Vol. I read for this entry — pp. 49, 204, 239, 460, 699, 710-711 and Appendix 7 — and the two sentences that come nearest, the satellite-photograph parenthesis at p. 699 and the centrally-located-Earth remark at p. 711, are both answered below. What the book does throughout is grant the phenomena and dispute their cause.' Then add a line to compression.note recording that p. 711 is the closest thing to a source for item 180 that was found, and that it contradicts the book's own p. 710.

findings.field: refutation, §2 final paragraph (cross-reference to ARG-B05); related[]
findings.problem: 'It is the same move the project records at ARG-B05, where he reproduces the Encyclopædia Britannica's correction for the curvature of the Earth and then denies the curvature it corrects for.' The subject of that sentence is Rowbotham, but clusters.py has B05 = 'Engineering makes no curvature allowance (canals, rail, pipelines, bridges)', originator William Carpenter, One Hundred Proofs, 1885 — a different author, a different book and no Britannica material. The finding described is B07 ('Refraction is invoked ad hoc to rescue curvature', Rowbotham, 1849, MISLEADING), whose treatment is built on Rowbotham reprinting the Encyclopædia Britannica 'Levelling' article with its one-seventh-of-the-curvature refraction coefficient at p. 34. The anchor is live, so a reader who clicks lands on Carpenter's canals and finds nothing of what the sentence promised.
findings.fix: Change the anchor and label to ARG-B07 and add 'B07' to related[]. Consider dropping 'B05' from related[] unless the Carpenter cluster is wanted for another reason.

findings.field: refutation, §3 first paragraph ('the French Peru and Lapland degrees (56,653 and 57,422 toises)'); docstring §6
findings.problem: The entry vouches for both figures — the docstring states they 'are the real published figures' — but only the Lapland one checks out. 57,422 toises is confirmed (and is exactly what the 1911 Britannica's Lapland arc of 55,023 toises over 57′ 29″·6 yields). The Peru figure does not: the same Britannica article gives the Peruvian arc as 176,945 toises over 3° 7′ 3″, i.e. about 56,760 toises per degree, and the figure in general circulation is 56,753. Rowbotham's 56,653 is roughly 100 toises (about 200 m) low — the same class of transposed digit as the '577 to 875' the paragraph three lines later is busy catching, and we certified it instead. The same sentence also asserts that both degrees 'did not survive later scrutiny intact'; Rowbotham's text and the sources reached here support that only for the Lapland arc.
findings.fix: Amend to: 'the Lapland degree he quotes, 57,422 toises, is the published Maupertuis figure and it did not survive the Swedish re-measurement intact; his Peru degree of 56,653 toises does not match the published Peruvian arc, which yields about 56,753-56,760 toises per degree — a second corrupt figure of the same kind as the Huygens ratio below, and a second one that inflates the disagreement his argument runs on.'

findings.field: refutation, §3 second-to-last paragraph ('overstates it by a factor of about 170')
findings.problem: The factor does not follow from any natural reading of the figures given. Rowbotham's 577:875 implies a flattening of (875−577)/875 = 0.3406, against Huygens's 1/578 = 0.001730 — a factor of about 197. Taking his own gloss ('about one-third of the whole diameter') gives 1/3 ÷ 1/578 ≈ 193. Reading 'it' as the Newton-Huygens disagreement rather than the flattening gives about 126. Nothing gives 170. The referent of 'it' is also unstated, which is half the problem: this is a published number a checker will recompute, in the one paragraph of the entry whose whole point is that an unchecked number was printed.
findings.fix: State the quantity and the arithmetic: 'his 577:875 implies a flattening of 0.34, about 197 times Huygens's actual 1/578 = 0.0017.'

findings.problem: The Noad coefficient is garbled inside a direct quotation. The HTML reads 'will alter its length ⅓<sub>5000</sub>th part', and ⅓ is U+2153 VULGAR FRACTION ONE THIRD, so the published gloss quotes Noad as saying '⅓5000th part'. The source (Gutenberg #69892, and the same sentence in the third edition) reads ¹⁄₅₀₀₀th part — one five-thousandth. The entity is two code points off (⅟ is ⅑). This is the load-bearing coefficient of the entry's centrepiece: a reader who wants to check 84.2 ÷ 150,000 cannot get 1/150,000 out of what the gloss prints, and the refutation four sections later gives the correct '1/5000 of its length for 30 °F', so the two disagree.
findings.fix: Replace with '1/5000th part' or '⅓' → '⅑<sub>5000</sub>th part', and check the rendered page rather than the entity table — the same ⅓ is used correctly as ⅓ in _b9_D19.py, which is probably where it was copied from.

findings.problem: The field that a reader meets side by side with the list's phrasing quotes, as Sungenis and Bennett's own wording, a sentence that is their statement of the geokinetic claim they are about to answer. On p. 710 the passage is introduced as 'there are three geokinetic claims for terrestrial motion' and 'All claims center on the inertial forces called centrifugal and Coriolis that explain the following effects ... based on the presumption of Earth's rotation'; the numbered item quoted is #2 in that opponent's list. The entry knows this — the gloss says 'states the geokinetic claim' and the note quotes the Response — but compression.source_wording carries the claim-statement alone with no marker, which is a small version of the move the hedge rule exists to stop, committed in our favour. The substance still holds: the Response at p. 711 concedes rather than denies, and that is what makes the drift finding stand.
findings.fix: Label it: 'Sungenis & Bennett, Vol. I ch. 12, p. 710, stating the geokinetic claim they will answer: centrifugal forces produce "the polar flattening and equatorial bulge. This also explains why the acceleration of gravity is less at the equator" — and answering it at p. 711 not by denying the effects but by writing that they "depend on the assumption that the inertial effects can only be caused by the Earth's rotation."'

findings.field: refutation, §6 ('The bulge is not stable, and the part that is unexplained does not help')
findings.problem: The section answers item 105's four-word fragment ('Stable equatorial bulge.') — no source wording for it is located anywhere in the entry — and it answers with variations whose magnitudes are never given, in an entry whose governing discipline is magnitude. The twice-daily body tide of about 30 cm is 1.4 × 10⁻⁵ of the 21.4 km bulge; the J2 reversal Cox and Chao report is of order 10⁻⁸ in relative terms, i.e. sub-millimetre on the polar-equatorial radius difference. 'It is not stable, and the ways in which it moves are among the better-measured things in geophysics' is true and well cited, but as an answer to 'stable' it is the kind of move the entry refuses to make elsewhere — and it sits three paragraphs from a passage arguing that a 113 m excess is negligible because it is half a per cent. The advocate block already anticipates the double-standard charge for the 113 m; it does not anticipate it here.
findings.fix: Add the ratios and reframe: 'the bulge is not rigid — it flexes about 30 cm twice a day, one part in 70,000 of its own size, and its dynamical measure J2 has a measured secular trend that reversed around 1998. These are small, and saying so is the point: they are exactly the size a responsive rotational figure should show, and none of them is available to an argument that needs the bulge to have a non-rotational cause.'

findings.problem: The one leg of the centrepiece not computed from the source's own numbers, and it answers a different mechanism than the one the source names. Rowbotham's second cause is resistance: 'if the pendulum vibrates in the air, which is colder and therefore denser in the north than at the equator, it must be more or less resisted in its passage through it', and his authority is Derham on the arcs of vibration in an air-pump receiver. Our reply invokes 'the buoyancy and added-mass corrections for a metal bob in air', gives no arithmetic, and asserts 'something of order a hundredth of one per cent' and 'two orders of magnitude below what is needed' with no derivation — while the steelman calls it 'several hundred times too small', a third figure. A defender gets to say we substituted a mechanism we could dismiss and then did not show the numbers, in the section whose authority comes from showing the numbers.
findings.fix: Name his mechanism and do the arithmetic in one line: buoyancy plus added mass shift the period by about ρ_air/ρ_bob ≈ 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ for a steel bob; the equator-to-pole change in sea-level air density is roughly 15-20% of that, so about 3 × 10⁻⁵ — a factor of ~150 short of 0.436%. Then note that damping, the effect Derham actually measured, changes amplitude and reaches the period only through the circular-error term, which is smaller still. Make the steelman's 'several hundred' agree with whichever number is published.

findings.problem: The published prose states Huygens's ratio flatly as 577:578 (flattening near 1/578), while the only authority the entry cites for the comparison — the 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica, 'Earth, Figure of the' — says 'the proportion of the axes should be 578 : 579', which is what sources[12] itself reports. The docstring records the variance; the prose does not, so a reader who follows the link finds our cited source disagreeing with our sentence by one. The scrambling observation (578 → 875) survives either way, since 577:578 is well attested elsewhere.
findings.fix: Add four words: 'Huygens's ratio was 577:578 — the 1911 Britannica states it as 578:579 — a flattening near 1/578, and 578 has plainly been scrambled into 875.'

findings.problem: pd=True, so the schema invites quoting at length, and the entry instead elides behind its two ellipses precisely the material the refutation's decisive step runs on: the Phillips temperature row (84.2 °F at the equator, 0.0 °F at the pole) and the Noad sentence with the 1/5000-per-30 °F coefficient. The reader meets both numbers only in our paraphrase, in the block that exists to let the source speak in its own voice. The first ellipsis also drops Rowbotham's flattest sentence — 'the essential evidence is wanting that the Earth is a globe at all! whether oblate or oblong, or truly spherical, are questions logically misplaced' — which is the sentence that licenses the gloss's claim that he denies the bulge is established rather than offering a rival cause for it.
findings.fix: Extend the quote (no fair-use cap applies) to carry the 'essential evidence is wanting' sentence and the two quoted figures, so the arithmetic in §2 is visibly performed on words the reader has already read.

findings.problem: The TLDR says the 747 "crossed New York to London eastbound in 4 h 56 min, at a ground speed of 1,327 km/h against an airspeed of 933." 1,327 km/h was the PEAK, not the crossing speed: the body itself says "an average ground speed of 1,126 km/h and a peak of 1,327 km/h", and Guinness says the aircraft reached "a speed of 1,327 km/h (825 mph) relative to the ground below". The TLDR's own numbers do not close — 5,554 km at 1,327 km/h is 4 h 11 min, not 4 h 56. This is the recurring failure the sweep report names twice (TLDR written from memory of the argument, stronger than the body), and it is in the field a reader sees before anything else and may never expand past.
findings.fix: Replace "at a ground speed of 1,327 km/h against an airspeed of 933" with "averaging 1,126 km/h over the ground and peaking at 1,327, against an airspeed of about 933".

findings.field: clusters.py A08 (renders into this entry's header and refutation summary)
findings.problem: clusters.py A08 still carries originator="Samuel Rowbotham", originator_work="Earth Not a Globe", year="1865", and note="Descends from Rowbotham's vertical-projectile argument. The atmosphere co-moves; INS platforms explicitly correct for a ~15 deg/hr Earth rate." render.py prints the originator in the meta line ("first published by …") directly above this treatment, and prints the cluster note as the refutation panel's summary line (build.py:161 maps note to basis; render.py renders basis under the "3 · Refutation" chip). So as shipped the page says "first published by Samuel Rowbotham" immediately above a gloss arguing the aeroplane argument cannot be Rowbotham's (he died 23 Dec 1884; powered flight 17 Dec 1903 — both verified), and summarises the refutation with "the atmosphere co-moves", the exact answer the entry's own steelman labels SURFACE and says "loses, and it deserves to". The file reports this upward in docstring note 10 and correctly does not edit another file, so this is a process defect, not a writing one — but it is unapplied, and it is the fifth recurrence of the E01/E03 pattern.
findings.fix: Owner outside this file: anchor the edit on the cluster key "A08" (never on the byte-identical originator= line), set the originator state deliberately — Henriet is the earliest text LOCATED, not a demonstrated first author, so untraced is the honest value unless a PER-HENRIET/WRK record is created and priority verified — and rewrite the note to lead with the alignment procedure rather than co-rotation. Then update tests/test_provenance.py: Rowbotham 65 → 61 items, plus the named-originator count and the Rowbotham+Sungenis 43% assertion.

findings.problem: Both fields say Henriet writes "kilometers" three times and Dubay prints "miles" three times. Inside the block Dubay reproduces it is FOUR times each: "1,000 kilometers an hour", "only 500 kilometers", "a distance of 1,500 kilometers", "such a flying speed of 1,000 kilometers an hour" — all four printed as miles. Henriet's fuller passage has a fifth ("an airfield which is slipping away at the rate of 1,000 kilometers an hour"), which the gloss itself quotes. The entry bills this substitution as its sharpest single finding; a defender with both texts open will find the count wrong on the first check.
findings.fix: "four times" in both fields, or "at every occurrence in the block he reproduces — four of them".

findings.field: compression.note ("verified in two independent copies of each book")
findings.problem: For Henriet this is true (archive.org item HeavenAndEarthGabrielleHenriet and the theflatearthsociety.org PDF — I confirmed "kilometers" in the second). For Dubay it is not: the file's own docstring note 4 says the two checks were "the djvu OCR and … the PDF text layer" of one Internet Archive item (200-proofs-the-earth-is-not-a-spinning-ball). Those are two derivations of a single scan, not two copies. On a page whose product is provenance rigour, overstating a verification claim is the most expensive kind of small error.
findings.fix: "verified in two independent copies of Henriet and in two text layers of the Internet Archive scan of Dubay".

findings.problem: The field is written with HTML entities (“, ”, —) but render.py escapes it: line 242 emits e(d["straw_man"]["detail"]) where e() is html.escape. The published paragraph will therefore read: gravity “magically and inexplicably drags the entire lower-atmosphere … infinite vacuum space.” — literal entity text throughout, in the one panel where we accuse the source of caricature. Every other treatment file writes literal typographic characters here; A08 and A19 are the only two that do not.
findings.fix: Replace “/”/— in straw_man.detail with the literal characters “ ” —, as _b8_R03.py and deep.py's A03 do.

findings.problem: The gloss says "East/west symmetry as a numbered proof is in One Hundred Proofs (1885) twice over" and then cites proof 44 and proof 54. Proof 54 (verified verbatim in Gutenberg #55387) is the balloon-not-left-behind argument and contains no east/west comparison at all — it is a vehicle-decoupling claim, the same family as the air-gun. The genuine second instance is proof 42 ("Projectiles--firing east or west": "there would unquestionably be a difference in the result of firing off a projectile in that direction and in a direction the opposite of that one. But as, in fact, there is not the slightest difference…"), which the docstring identifies but the published gloss drops. A defender who opens the cited Gutenberg text finds our claimed ancestry citing a proof that never mentions east or west.
findings.fix: "…is in One Hundred Proofs (1885) twice over — proof 42 and, restated with a figure, proof 44", then keep proof 54 introduced as what it is: the balloon form of the same decoupling argument.

findings.problem: unsourced_addition is justified on the ground that "the symmetry claim is attributed to a literature in which this pass could not locate it". But Dubay proof 24 — one item before the quoted run, in the same book — asserts directional symmetry as observed fact: "regardless of which direction cannons are fired, the distance covered is always the same." Carpenter proof 44, quoted in our own gloss, asserts it too ("there is not the slightest difference, whichever way the thing may be done"). By the entry's own genealogical logic (docstring: "the vehicle is a cannon and a balloon because those were the vehicles") the symmetry claim IS in that literature, with a different vehicle. The entry quotes proofs 23, 25, 26 and 27 and never mentions 24, the nearest counter-example to its own classification.
findings.fix: Address proof 24 in the note and say why cannon symmetry is not flight-time symmetry, or reclassify as scope_widened (which the note already offers as the alternative) and keep unsourced_addition only for item 13's "navigation not compensating".

findings.field: refutation section 1 ("westbound traffic detoured north of Greenland")
findings.problem: "On the same day westbound traffic detoured north of Greenland to escape the headwind and lost more than an hour." No source in the sources list carries this: the Guinness page covers only the eastbound record (confirmed on fetch), and the CNN piece has nothing about 9 February westbound routings (confirmed on fetch). The supporting source is the Flightradar24 record-flight post, cited in docstring note 5 but absent from sources. That post also says less than we do: "flights are routing to the north of the jet stream over Greenland" and "Some flights are adding more than 60 minutes, while others that manage to avoid the jet stream entirely are in some cases arriving early." We flatten "some flights" into "westbound traffic" and drop the early arrivals — a small compression of a hedged source, in an entry about compression of hedged sources.
findings.fix: Add the Flightradar24 post to sources and rewrite as: "the same day, westbound flights were routing north of the jet stream over Greenland, some adding more than an hour."

findings.problem: https://digilander.libero.it/andreatheone/irs.htm returns HTTP 410 Gone (checked twice this run, default and browser user-agent; the Libero portal page is served instead), and the Wayback availability API returned no snapshot for it. This is the load-bearing citation for the entry's headline TLDR claim and for five quoted sentences in section 3. The text itself is fine — I verified every quoted sentence, including "These comparisons must be favorable to complete the alignment period", against a live mirror carrying the identical document.
findings.fix: Cite http://b767ops.blogspot.com/2014/06/about-irss-and-how-they-work.html (live, same text, same five sentences) alongside or instead of the digilander URL, keeping the "unofficial mirror" disclosure and the Inside GNSS corroboration.

findings.problem: Section 5 states flatly that Coriolis, Eötvös, sensed Earth rate and the clock split are "four quantities that are zero on a stationary Earth", and section 4 says the Hafele–Keating split "exists only because the ground the aircraft take off from is itself moving". The entry's own advocate rates the rotating-cosmos reply 4/5 and its preemptive (c) commits to conceding it "in the body with a cross-link to ARG-R01 and ARG-R03" — narrowly, because neither list claim survives the concession. That concession is not in the body: the refutation cross-links R03 only for the weaker Galilean cancelling point and never mentions R01. And build.py strips advocate from the published deep (it is written to review/advocate.json), so a reader sees the unqualified claim and never the concession. The physics is right; the strongest attack on the entry is answered only where readers cannot see it.
findings.fix: Add two sentences to section 5: concede that the gyro, Coriolis and clock results measure rotation relative to the local inertial frame and are observationally equivalent under a rotating-cosmos model (link ARG-R01 and ARG-R03), then narrow — "flight times symmetric" is false in the timetables and "navigation not compensating" is false in the alignment procedure whatever defines that frame.

findings.problem: "This is the same instrument, and the same 15°/hr, that ARG-A07 records a flat-earth researcher measuring on camera and declining to accept." Two problems. (a) "The same instrument" follows immediately after naming the Honeywell GG1320AN; _b8_A07.py identifies no model for Knodel's gyro and deliberately withholds even the widely-quoted price line, so we have no basis for identity of instrument, only of type. (b) "Declining to accept" is the framing A07 explicitly abandons: A07 credits the systematics hunt as "correct practice", locates its finding in a missing acceptance criterion, and lists "you have written it up as refusing to accept data" as the defender's charge against us. Knodel is living, and A07 is scrupulous about it; A08 reimports the framing in one clause.
findings.fix: "This is the same quantity, and the same instrument class — a navigation-grade ring laser gyro — that ARG-A07 records reading 15°/hr on camera, where the finding is the missing acceptance criterion rather than the reading."

findings.problem: Four small precision slips, none affecting the argument. (1) The locator calls the Internet Archive item "the print edition"; the item's metadata carries no publisher, date or edition statement (uploader-supplied 2023 scan, tesseract OCR), so the edition is asserted rather than shown — and edition/dating is this project's third recurring failure class. (2) "The thing being measured is about four thousand times the instrument's noise floor" follows the 9.36°/hr horizontal figure, against which 0.0035°/hr gives ~2,700; 4,300 is the ratio to the full 15.041°/hr — and bias stability is not strictly a noise floor. (3) compression.note says Henriet "offers no empirical observation in the passage Dubay reproduces", but that passage contains one — a flying speed of 1,000 an hour "has recently been achieved"; the load-bearing clause that follows (flight times are not stated in it) is correct. (4) Section 2's "which is why the mid-latitude belt blows from the southwest" holds in the northern hemisphere only, in a paragraph whose point is hemispheric symmetry; and the gloss truncates Henriet's chapter II title without an ellipsis (it continues "and on the existence of a day and of a night cosmic breath stream").
findings.fix: Say "the Internet Archive scan" rather than "the print edition"; attach the ratio to the quantity it uses ("about 4,300 times the gyro's typical bias stability"); narrow (3) to "no observation of flight times"; add "in the northern hemisphere" and an ellipsis to the chapter title.

findings.problem: "No physicist since 1905 has held that." — held, that is, that some experiment has proved the Earth to be in absolute motion. Dayton Miller held exactly that: his Mount Wilson interferometry programme ran into the 1930s and his summary paper is titled "The Ether-Drift Experiment and the Determination of the Absolute Motion of the Earth" (Rev. Mod. Phys. 5:203, 1933). He was a credentialed physicist, not a crank on the margins, and he is item 100 of this very list ("Miller aether drift detections."), which our own §6 names. straw_man.detail renders escaped into a published box, so the defender gets to quote our page against our page.
findings.fix: Rescope to the mainstream and name the exception before they do: "...the position attacked is that some experiment has proved the Earth to be in absolute motion. Mainstream physics has not made that claim since 1905, and the last credentialed physicist to press it — Dayton Miller, whose drift claim is item 100 of this same list — is the exception the movement itself cites."

findings.problem: The entry establishes that the DOCTRINE was in the 1992 edition and never tests whether Bouw ORIGINATED it, yet the record credits him and the entry publishes a pedigree ("Where item 310 comes from", "item 310's pedigree runs through a citation Bouw gets right") with no hedge on origination. The entry's own quoted sentence undercuts the credit: at p. 4 Bouw attributes the proposition to "the more subtle physicists", i.e. explicitly to other people — the gloss even says so — and note 6 concedes item 318 cannot be tied to him at all. So one of three items is not his and the other two are, on his own page, someone else's. On a project whose product is provenance and whose README requires origin in three states with "untraced rather than guessed" as a live option, that omission is the error the C02 correction exists to prevent. (A parallel batch-11 treatment of the same cluster reaches the opposite provenance conclusion; the git history records the double-booking as unresolved, so this is the comparison the merge was deferred for.)
findings.fix: Add to the gloss, in the project's own vocabulary: "What is established here is that the doctrine is Bouw's in print, not that it is Bouw's in origin. He attributes the proposition on p. 4 to 'the more subtle physicists', item 318 could not be located in this text at all, and no earlier claimant was tested in this pass — so the origination credit in our record is provisional and is published as such." Report the originator field upward rather than editing it here.

findings.field: clusters.py R11 note (renders as the `basis` line beside the verdict chip)
findings.problem: The summary line readers see before expanding says Bouw "conceded his model is observationally equivalent to heliocentrism and must therefore be chosen on theological grounds." That states as Bouw's settled position one horn of the contradiction this entry exists to expose, and the entry's §3 says the opposite — that he asserts a falsifiable cosmology in the body of the book. The source backs §3: p. 3 "every fundamental experiment ever devised to measure the speed of the earth through space measures a speed of zero"; p. 4 "the geocentric evidence is overwhelming"; p. 523 "Geocentricity predicts that earth's lack of motion is absolute"; p. 556 the chapter-36 phenomena "point to a geocentric universe"; p. 539 "the preponderance of geocentric evidence in cosmology has finally forced a geocentric-type model". The theological concession is real but narrow — the Earth-versus-Milky-Way residual at p. 556 and the Bible-believer sufficiency claim at p. 15 — and the note generalises it into Bouw's whole position. This is recurring failure #5, in the highest-traffic field on the entry.
findings.fix: Replace with a note that states both horns: "Bouw states the symmetry himself — dynamical proofs 'are not proofs of anything; nor are they proofs against the geocentric universe' — and elsewhere in the same book calls the geocentric evidence overwhelming and reports his model as making predictions that experiments confirm. The list files the first claim as a proof while spending the second. Where the astronomical evidence runs out, at the Earth-versus-Galaxy gap, he names Scripture as what closes it."

findings.problem: Two printed-page locators are off by one. I settled both from rendered page images, not OCR. (a) The Sagnac sentence — "been performed accurately enough to discern the period of absolute rotation of the firmament is the sidereal day" — is on printed p. 522 (running head "522 Chapter 35"); p. 523 begins with the head "Rotation 523" further down the leaf. The "Geocentricity predicts..." quotes in the same sentence of our text ARE on p. 523, so the refutation attributes two quotes a page apart to one page. (b) The Milky-Way / Scripture concession — "could just as well be viewed as located at the center of the cosmic shells ... But that is where Scripture comes into play" — is on printed p. 556 (running head "556 Chapter 36"), not p. 555; it is the closing paragraph of chapter 36 and the chapter ends on that page.
findings.fix: In §3, split the citation: "...at p. 523 the model is stated as making predictions in so many words ... and, a page earlier, Sagnac interferometry is said to have 'been performed accurately enough...' (p. 522)." Change "(ch. 36, p. 555)" to "(ch. 36, p. 556)" in the steelman and in §5's reference to chapter 36. In sources[0].label, change "Sagnac and the firmament's rotation p. 523" to "the firmament's predicted rotation p. 523 and the Sagnac sidereal-day claim p. 522", and "the Milky-Way concession p. 555" to "p. 556".

findings.problem: The TLDR says the construction's "Earth-near-centre versions were in severe tension with the data by 2011", flat. The body's own limit paragraph says the opposite about scope: "What is established is narrower than 'we are not near a centre': it is that the specific Gpc-scale inhomogeneous models proposed as a replacement for dark energy do badly against the data" — and it quotes Zibin & Moss saying the headline kSZ constraint is "considerably weakened (though still impressive)". The TLDR generalises from dark-energy-replacement void models to all Earth-near-centre versions and drops the caveat the body was careful to publish. This is the recurring TLDR-outruns-body pattern, in the field readers see first and may never expand past.
findings.fix: "...and whose Gpc-scale void versions — the ones proposed as a replacement for dark energy — were in severe tension with the data by 2011."

findings.problem: Bouw's own hedge on the Ellis material is nowhere recorded, and it runs in two directions at once. At p. 539 he writes that "Ellis' model has become an oddity among cosmological models, and it is not without its problems; but it is interesting to see that the preponderance of geocentric evidence in cosmology has finally forced a geocentric-type model, albeit the earth is there placed opposite the center." So (i) he qualifies the very construction we present his citation as cleanly transmitting, and (ii) he reads it not as underdetermination but as evidence forcing a conclusion — which is nearer the opposite of item 310 and is stronger support for our verdict than anything in §6. Separately, the p. 92 quotation that chapter 36 note 2 actually attaches to is Ellis on the cosmological principle being "assumed for a priori reasons and not tested by observation", not the abstract's equivalence result; our gloss reads as though note 2 carries the construction.
findings.fix: In the gloss, after the note-2 sentence: "The note is attached to a different Ellis sentence — the cosmological principle is 'assumed for a priori reasons and not tested by observation' — and where Bouw discusses the construction itself, at pp. 538–539, he calls it 'an oddity among cosmological models' that 'is not without its problems', reading it as a model the evidence 'finally forced' rather than as one of several that fit. That last reading is the tension in a sentence: a claim that the evidence decides, printed twenty pages from the claim that nothing can." Add the hedge to compression.note.

findings.problem: "Appendix E derives the rotating-frame accelerations (eq. 11) and stops there" is false about the appendix's contents, and preemptive (a) insists this claim "must stay a statement about what the appendix contains". It does not stop: immediately after the p. 746 sentence we quote, Bouw writes "Of course, equation (11) is kinematic, not dynamic and we have to show the geocentric model is dynamically correct. To do that, all we have to do is to multiply both sides by the star's mass, m", producing eq. (12) F = ma, and then applies it to the sun, moon, planets, artificial satellites, stars and to light propagation. Worse for §3: the appendix OPENS (pp. 740–741, eqs. 1–3) by arguing that the kinematic/dynamic distinction is a "sleight of hand" — multiplying one side by m/m — which is Bouw's pre-emptive answer to our "his cosmos is not a relabelling", and it goes unengaged. Not published (build strips advocate to review/advocate.json), but it is the stated reason we run no fit against Bouw's model, so it will misdirect the next editor.
findings.fix: Correct the note to what is true: "Appendix E (pp. 740–747) ends at F = ma for a single star (eq. 12); no field equation, stress-energy tensor or cosmological solution appears anywhere in it, so there is no fit to run." And add one sentence to §3 answering the m/m argument on its merits: what makes the model dynamical is not the factor of m but the claim at p. 5 that a superdense medium "physically controls all motion" and at p. 746 that its gravitational field is what holds the star in place — a medium with a gravitational field is not a bookkeeping convention, whichever side of the equation the mass sits on.

findings.problem: The p. 4 quotation is elided as "The more subtle physicists … will claim, with some justification...". What the ellipsis removes is not connective tissue but the clause "many of whom know well that the geocentric evidence is overwhelming" — from inside the quoted sentence, and it substantially weakens the hedged reading we build on it. The gloss does disclose the clause, but locates it as "the same page", which understates the cut: it is the same sentence, indeed the elided span. compression.source_wording repeats the elision with no disclosure at all, and that block is the side-by-side comparison a reader uses to check us. Given that this entry's own standing rule is not to commit the compression sin in our favour, the elision needs to be visible where the comparison is made.
findings.fix: In the gloss change "the same page tells the reader" to "the elided clause itself tells the reader", and quote it in place: "The more subtle physicists, [many of whom know well that the geocentric evidence is overwhelming,] will claim, with some justification...". Restore the bracketed clause to compression.source_wording so the comparison block shows what was cut.

findings.problem: Two absence claims are asserted unscoped, in fields the ratchet test reads. "No result in this literature locates a planet" is a claim about an entire literature made from five papers; "That result was never retracted" is a claim about the whole record of a journal. Both are substantively right, and neither matches the banned regex — which is precisely the failure the last sweep described as "writers have learned the regex, not the rule". The house rule is to name the text searched.
findings.fix: "None of the results cited above — Alnes & Amarzguioui, Caldwell & Stebbins, Clarkson/Bassett/Lu, Zhang & Stebbins, Moss/Zibin/Scott — constrains an observer's position at better than megaparsec resolution; at that resolution the Earth and the Milky Way are the same point." And: "No retraction or erratum is attached to the paper on the publisher's record page, which is where we looked."

findings.problem: "filed beside forty items claiming that the experiments came out one way" is a numeric claim published on the page with no test behind it and no derivable definition, which the README forbids. Counted narrowly — the clusters that assert an experimental result favouring geocentrism (A01, A02, A03, A06, A07, A11, A12, A19, A26) — the figure is 21. Counted as the whole A-EXP lane it is 101. Forty is defensible under some intermediate reading but not derivable from the dataset, so it cannot be pinned by a test.
findings.fix: Use a figure the build can produce and test: "filed beside the twenty-one items on this list that assert an experiment came out the geocentrist's way", and add the assertion to tests/test_provenance.py alongside the existing cluster-count checks.

findings.problem: Faulkner's review is cited as "Journal of Creation 15(2), 2001". In 2001 the journal was Creation Ex Nihilo Technical Journal; it was renamed Journal of Creation in 2006, and creation.com retro-labels the archive. Bouw's own chapter 4 note 1 in the book we are quoting cites it as "Creation Ex Nihilo Technical Journal, 15(2):110-121". On a project that has already been bitten twice by edition and volume dating, the contemporaneous name is the safer one.
findings.fix: "Faulkner, 'Geocentrism and Creation', Creation Ex Nihilo Technical Journal 15(2):110–121, 2001 (archived by the publisher as Journal of Creation)".

findings.problem: "Bouw invokes inflation approvingly at p. 104, as the mechanism by which starlight reaches a young Earth." The page runs the argument in the other direction: the question posed is "The sun is only six billion years old; how can its light extend to the outer edge of space some 13 to 20 billion light years out?", answered by God stretching out the heaven, "Modern astronomy refers to that as inflation". The young-universe payoff on that page is about apparent versus true age ("an apparent nuclear age of twenty billion years but with a true age of 6,000 years"), not about distant starlight arriving here.
findings.fix: "...invokes inflation approvingly at p. 104, as the stretching of the heavens that lets the sun's light already reach the edge of a universe whose true age he puts at 6,000 years."

findings.problem: The entry's headline claim — Rowbotham "measured it with a theodolite, conceded the reading" for the SEA-HORIZON dip — is sourced to THEODOLITE TANGENT, which is not about the sea horizon. In that section "the above" refers to a spirit-level/graduated-staff experiment over 100 chains with repeated back and fore sights; the concession is about the levelling result, not the dip. Worse, the section immediately following it, TANGENTIAL HORIZON (never mentioned anywhere in the file), is where he does discuss the sea horizon with a theodolite — and it ends by denying exactly what we put in his mouth: "This angle, A, T, H, is never observed, but always A, T, S, plus collimation or divergence produced by the lenses in the telescope of the theodolite." We quote to a concession and stop one section before the flat denial, which is the hedge rule violated in our favour.
findings.fix: Requote from where he actually says it. Experiment 11, printed p. 41 (sacred-texts za16.htm): "he has been challenged by surveyors to make use of the theodolite, or ordinary 'spirit level' ... In every instance when the experiment was tried, this appearance was found to exist" — that is the theodolite concession, and it is stronger than the one we used. Add TANGENTIAL HORIZON's "From the above, which is perfectly true" (he concedes the dip grows with altitude) AND its "This angle, A, T, H, is never observed", then answer that denial. Keep the THEODOLITE TANGENT quote only if the body says what "the above" refers to.

findings.problem: The steelman omits the source's actual empirical backing and thereby leaves our best discriminator unanswered. At Experiment 11 (printed pp. 41-42) Rowbotham does not merely assert collimation — he builds a lens-free control: an iron tube about 18 inches long, closed but for "a very small aperture", cross-hairs at the far end, spirit level attached, and reports that the cross-hair "was seen to cut or to fall close to the horizon ... tried in various places, and at different altitudes, and always with the same result." That is a null result from a non-telescopic instrument at varying altitude, i.e. a direct pre-emption of our sqrt(h) argument ("carry the same instrument from 2 m to 100 m and the reading must grow sevenfold"). A well-informed defender opens with it, and the page has no reply.
findings.fix: Put the iron-tube control in the KERNEL, then answer it on resolution: a pinhole a millimetre across at 18 inches subtends about 7.5', and a spider-line cross-hair a few arcminutes, so the apparatus cannot resolve the 2.5'-10.6' dips available at the heights he used — it is a null with no power, not a null result. Say so with the numbers, since that is the same move we make about the naked eye elsewhere in the entry.

findings.field: refutation §2 and steelman.why_it_doesnt_save_claim — the three discriminators (lines 215-218, 232)
findings.problem: The strongest refutation of the collimation defence is inside the passage the entry already quotes, and the entry misses it. At Experiment 11, printed p. 43, Rowbotham quotes J. F. Heather, A Treatise on Mathematical Instruments, on adjusting collimation: "The instrument will now be in complete practical adjustment for any distance not exceeding ten chains (220 yards), the maximum error being only 1/1000 of a foot." That is 0.001 ft at 660 ft = 1.5e-6 rad = 0.31 arcsecond. He needs collimation to produce 6.2' (372") of dip at his own 34-foot pier and up to 22" of spherical excess on a 100 km triangle. His own cited authority caps the effect three orders of magnitude below what his explanation requires. All three of our current discriminators are external to him (reversal convention, sqrt(h), area scaling); this one is internal and needs nothing a reader has to take on trust.
findings.fix: Add a fourth discriminator, first in the list: quote the Heather line as Rowbotham quotes it, do the division (0.31" vs 372"), and note that it is his own footnote. Cite it as 1881, 3rd ed., Experiment 11, p. 43.

findings.problem: "...at the heights his own experiments were done at the dip is a few arcminutes, which is why his witnesses did not see it" is contradicted by the body two clauses later and by the gloss. The witnesses are the balloonists (Wise, Mayhew, Elliott, the London Journal, Glaisher) at one and a half to two miles, where the entry itself computes 1.82 degrees — not arcminutes — and where the body's actual explanation is the absence of any levelled reference in a swinging basket, not smallness. Experiment 10 (his own experiment) is the balloon case too. The TLDR is escaped and sits above the fold, so this is the sentence most readers will take away, and it hands a defender the reply the advocate block already anticipates ("if 1.8 degrees is hard to see, the balloon testimony tells us nothing either way").
findings.fix: Split the two populations: "...on a pier or a hotel roof the dip is a few arcminutes, below what an eye with no levelled reference can judge; from a balloon two miles up his own figures give 1.8 degrees, and the reason his witnesses still reported eye level is that a swinging basket carries no horizontal reference at all." Also soften "it is 1.75 arcminutes times the square root of the height in metres", which the body correctly presents as the refracted value against a geometric 1.93' with k varying.

findings.problem: "on the perspective account he actually holds, the visible range is fixed by an object's size against the eye's acuity and has no dependence on the observer's height whatever" is a claim about their theory that their text does not support and that does not survive formalisation. Carpenter's proof 32 ties the vanishing point to objects "no higher than we stand — say, six feet", i.e. to the observer's height; and on a flat plane an acuity-limited horizon scales as sqrt(h) too, because ground detail at distance d subtends roughly h*delta/d^2, giving d = sqrt(h*delta/epsilon). Once its one free constant is fitted to "about three miles" at 6 feet, that model reproduces 200 miles at 26,700 ft as well as sqrt(2Rh) does. So the two-point fit is not the discriminator §5 says it is.
findings.fix: Drop "no dependence on the observer's height whatever". Replace the discrimination claim with what the perspective account genuinely cannot do: it has a free parameter where sqrt(2Rh) has none, and it must also predict the dip, the sextant correction and the spherical excess with the same constant. Or move §5's weight onto the fact that sqrt(2Rh) is fixed by an independently measured R.

findings.problem: "Carpenter supplies two, sixty-six-fold apart ... Both of his numbers are on the curve" reads as an exhaustive account of his horizon figures, and the same proof we quote supplies a third: proof 6 says that from "Federal Hill, Baltimore, we may see twenty-five miles away, on a level with the eye". Federal Hill is roughly 80-100 ft above the harbour, for which sqrt(2Rh) gives 11-12 miles. A defender checking our own citation finds a number in it that is not on the curve, in the sentence right after the one we quote.
findings.fix: Say "two he states as horizon distances" and deal with the third explicitly: it is a visibility claim about distant objects, not a sea-horizon distance, and it is exactly the B04 long-range-visibility material — which is where it should be cross-linked.

findings.problem: "Every observation in the chapter is consistent with a sphere" is an unscoped universal about ch. II, and the chapter contains observations that are not. Experiment 12 (printed p. 44) reports a Dublin steamer's masthead still visible after four hours from a telescope 6 ft above the water — at least 32 miles — which on a sphere would need a masthead about 550 ft high. Experiment 8 claims a 22-mile straight base line for the Isle of Wight and a 50-mile view of the Welsh coast. Those are B04's business and are answered there by refraction and by misreporting, not by "consistent with a sphere".
findings.fix: Scope it to the experiments actually under discussion: "Every observation in Experiments 7, 11 and 15 is consistent with a sphere, and the sphere is what predicts they would come out that way." Cross-link the long-range visibility experiments to B04.

findings.problem: We restate the source's restriction as being about "unaided sight" / "the unaided eye", but the source's own words are "unless some telescopic instrument is used" — a restriction about lenses, not about instruments. The difference is material and the counter-examples are in the sentences we cite: the DIP SECTOR passage itself rests the claim on "experiments 10 and 11 ... and experiment 15", and Experiment 15 is a levelled CLINOMETER, while Experiment 11's control is a lens-free tube with cross-hairs and a spirit level. So "Everything Rowbotham offers in its support is unaided" is false, and the compression finding ("a claim stated for the unaided eye is applied to instrument and camera observation") slightly inflates the drift in our favour.
findings.fix: Use his category, not ours: the claim is scoped to NON-TELESCOPIC observation, which is why he can offer a clinometer and a lens-free tube inside it. The compression finding survives unchanged and more cleanly, because Dubay's proof 1 rests on "balloon, rocket, plane and drone footage", which is lens-mediated by construction.

findings.problem: The label says "Herschel, A Treatise on Astronomy (1833), pp. 15-18" but the linked archive item (atreatiseonastr01hersgoog) is the 1838 Carey, Lea & Blanchard Philadelphia printing, where the dip-sector passage is at printed pp. 21-23 (sections 20-22; printed p. 16 is section 14, on apparent versus real motion). The page range is Rowbotham's own footnote ("'Treatise on Astronomy,' pp. 15 to 18"), presented here as our citation. This is the edition-dating trap the sweep flags as recurring failure 3, and a reader who follows our link to check the quotation finds nothing at those pages.
findings.fix: Either link an 1833 London printing and verify pp. 15-18 there, or keep this scan and write: "Herschel, A Treatise on Astronomy, sections 20-22 (pp. 21-23 in the 1838 Philadelphia printing linked here; Rowbotham cites 'pp. 15 to 18' of the edition he used)."

findings.problem: The preemptive states that both commitments are "already in the body", and commitment (1) is that the refraction concession is stated "with a number and a condition — k = 1 requires an inversion of about 0.13 K/m sustained along the sightline". No such number or condition appears in the refutation; the second concession paragraph gives the k quote and "at k = 1 the dip vanishes entirely" and stops. The 0.13 K/m figure exists only in docstring note 8, which no reader sees. Since the advocate block renders, the page tells a reader something about itself that is not true — the same failure mode as shipping a recommendation as a finding.
findings.fix: Either add the number to the refutation's second concession paragraph ("k = 1 needs roughly a 0.13 K/m inversion sustained along the sightline — real over cold water, in a shallow layer, transiently, and not in every azimuth at once"), or rewrite the preemptive to say the commitment is required rather than already met.

findings.problem: "it does sit within a few arcminutes of eye level at any height a person can stand on" and "The dip at any height a person reaches unaided is genuinely below the threshold of unaided judgement" are unscoped universals that our own citations falsify. The Herschel passage we quote names Etna, Teneriffe and Mowna Roa — 1.7 to 1.9 degrees of dip — and a person can stand on Everest, where it is 2.7 degrees. The examples actually supporting the sentence (2.5', 6.2', 10.6') are all sea-level-to-cliff heights.
findings.fix: Scope to the heights the argument is about: "at any height reachable on foot from a shoreline — a beach, a pier, a hundred-foot cliff — it is a few arcminutes", and note that from a high mountain it is degrees, which is Herschel's point in the passage Rowbotham is answering.

findings.problem: Quotation merging in both directions. straw_man.detail attributes "gradually, noticeably decline towards the extremities" to Rowbotham's Experiment 7 as well as Dubay's proof 60; that wording is Dubay's. Refutation §4 attributes "gradually decline from the centre" to both; that wording is Rowbotham's. §4 also says Experiment 7 "survives verbatim into Dubay's proof 60", which the docstring (note 1) and the compression note correctly call "reworded" — Dubay rewrites throughout and gives 66.6 feet where Rowbotham gives 66 feet 8 inches.
findings.fix: Attribute each phrase to its own text and change "survives verbatim" to "survives almost intact" or "reworded, down to the same 66-foot figure", matching the docstring.

findings.problem: "1 m -> 1.93' geometric; Young's refracted 1.75'; the ~9% is refraction at k~=0.13" gets the coefficient wrong. Refracted dip scales as sqrt(1-k), so 1.75/1.926 implies k = 0.17-0.18; k = 0.13 gives 1.80'. Young's page says k is "about 1/6 or 1/7 at sea level" and separately notes 0.13 is the value long used in surveying — the two are being conflated. This is the block a later agent will copy numbers out of.
findings.fix: Write "the ~9% is refraction at k ~= 0.17 (sqrt(1-k) = 1.75/1.93); Young notes surveyors have long used k ~= 0.13, which would give 1.80'."

findings.problem: "the drop in feet is in his text, the angle is not" is an absence claim with no scope, in the field readers see first. The body scopes the same claim properly ("the ratio is not taken anywhere in that section", "did not take anywhere in the section"), so the TLDR is weaker than the work behind it.
findings.fix: "...the drop in feet is in the Experiment 11 passage; the angle is not."

findings.field: steelman.why_it_doesnt_save_claim, refutation section 3, sources[] label for USNO
findings.problem: The phrase quoted three times as the US Naval Observatory's — "a nominal horizontal refraction of 34 minutes" — is not on the cited page. https://aa.usno.navy.mil/faq/RST_defs (fetched 2026-08-11) reads: "The 50-arcminute geometric depression of the Sun's center used for the computations is obtained by adding the average apparent radius of the Sun (16 arcminutes) to the average amount of atmospheric refraction at the horizon (34 arcminutes)." The quoted wording is Andrew Young's, on https://aty.sdsu.edu/explain/sunset_time.html — "the sum of an average radius of 16 minutes, and a nominal horizontal refraction of 34 minutes" — a page this entry already cites for something else. The substance (a fixed 34′, published in advance, used worldwide) is fully supported by USNO; only the quotation is misattributed. On a provenance project a quoted string attributed to a source that does not contain it is the exact charge we level at the list, and it sits in the sources[] label a reader would click to check.
findings.fix: Either quote USNO in its own words — 90.8333 degrees, and "the average amount of atmospheric refraction at the horizon (34 arcminutes)" — or keep the phrase and attribute it correctly: "what Andrew Young calls 'a nominal horizontal refraction of 34 minutes'". Fix the sources[] label the same way.

findings.problem: An unscoped absence claim about the whole book, in three fields, where the body scopes it correctly. TLDR: "on the one magnitude his book supplies for it". Steelman: "It is never measured." Advocate: "the correction he substitutes has one magnitude in the whole book". The refutation says the scoped, defensible thing — "The one magnitude he supplies for it, in the chapters read for this entry" — and the entry read ch. II and the SPHERICAL EXCESS / TANGENTIAL HORIZON sections of a 430-page third edition, not the book. This is failure mode 1 in review/curmudgeon.md migrating into the fields the ratchet does not scan, and it is in the TLDR, which is read first.
findings.fix: TLDR: "…is, on the only magnitude the chapters read for this entry supply, about 240 times too small." Steelman: replace "It is never measured." with "No measurement of it is located in the chapters read for this entry." Advocate (d): "the correction he substitutes has one magnitude in the chapters read here".

findings.field: refutation section 5 ("The discrepancy he needs it to absorb is his own figure: 11 feet 8 inches of expected drop for the fig. 3 experiment at p. 35")
findings.problem: This misdescribes his position at the one place it names. In the fig. 3 experiment Rowbotham reports that no drop was seen and treats the absence as proof; he needs to absorb nothing there, so collimation is not offered against that 11 ft 8 in. The places he actually deploys instrumental "refraction, or … collimation" are the horizon dip (za16), the Ordnance Survey's spherical excess (za43, p. 263), and the 1870 Bedford Level result, where at za45 p. 272 he calls it "fully sufficient to explain the position of the disc at B, and the flag at C" — an observed offset of order five to six feet, not eleven feet eight. A well-informed defender gets a free hit here: "you sized my substitute against a discrepancy I never asked it to explain." The conclusion is robust across all three cases (factors of roughly 100 to 600), so only the pairing needs repair, not the arithmetic.
findings.fix: Anchor the comparison to a case he actually applies it to, or reframe the yardstick: "…about half an inch. For collimation to stand in for curvature at that range it has to be able to produce what curvature produces there — on his own figures, 11 feet 8 inches over six miles, and the several feet he calls it 'fully sufficient' to explain in the 1870 Bedford result at p. 272. His substitute is short by a factor of roughly 240 against the first and of order 100 against the second."

findings.field: verdict_challenge.reasoning (rendered on the page via render.py line 234)
findings.problem: "item 263, 'Mirage optical ducts.', asserts atmospheric ducting as a mechanism in its own right, four items after 221 charges that invoking it is illegitimate." Item 263 is forty-two items after item 221, not four (checked against scripts/corpus.py ITEMS and scripts/assign.py ASSIGN: 221 -> B07, 222 -> B04, 223 -> B06, 263 -> B13). findings.problem: The compression block runs Dubay's proof 71 as source wording for item 221 and then reasons from it — "Both sources hedge and the item does not… Four words on the list carry neither the concession, nor the experiment, nor the photograph the objection was about" — which asserts that item 221 descends from a proof about Joshua Nowicki's photograph. findings.fix: Demote the Dubay half from source to parallel: "The nearest modern form of the same charge is Dubay's proof 71, though item 221's descent from it is not traced here — and it hedges the same way: 'while these certainly do occur…'". Leave the drift_type computed on the Rowbotham comparison, which is documented.

findings.problem: The Dubay quotation is cut mid-sentence at "unlike a hazy illusory mirage" with a closing quote and no ellipsis, in both fields. findings.fix: Close the quotation with the rest of the sentence in both places: "…unlike a hazy illusory mirage, and on a ball-Earth 25,000 miles in circumference should be 2,400 feet below the horizon." findings.field: passage.gloss ("He allows for it, three separate times" / "applies it to every row of his lighthouse table"); repeated in compression.note and verdict_challenge.reasoning
findings.problem: Two loose quantifiers a defender can check in a minute. (a) Of the three instances listed, only two are allowances he makes — the one-twelfth deduction and the Experiment 3 theodolite reading; the third is his reprinting of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, which supplies the mechanism but is not an allowance of his. (b) In the 1881 text he states that the allowance is the only modification that can be made to the calculations and then works exactly one row: "Take the last case as an instance. The altitude of the light on Cape Bonavista, Newfoundland, is 150 feet, which, divided by 12, gives 13 feet as the amount to be deducted from 491 feet" (za14). "Applies it to every row" overstates a single worked deduction; nothing in the argument needs more than one.
