findings.field: refutation, second paragraph ("Second, the ledger, and it is Rowbotham's") + tldr, second sentence
findings.problem: The ledger — the entry's central positive claim, repeated in the closing verdict paragraph and paraphrased in the TLDR — counts Rowbotham's chapter titles rather than his chapters, and counts the two sides on different scales. (1) We say the contents page assigns "a separate chapter, and a separate mechanism" to "the cause of day and night and the seasons (VI)". Rowbotham's Section 6 says the opposite in its own words: "Thus, day and night, long and short days, Winter and Summer, the long periods of alternate light and darkness at the pole, arise simply from the Sun's position in relation to the north pole" — i.e. VI is derived from IV and V, exactly the move we credit the globe with. It is not an independent stipulation, so "six stipulations against two" is five at best. (2) The same paragraph lists XIII among costs "still to be paid for separately", but Section 13 runs on the same convergence-of-parallels principle as Section 7 ("horizontal lines parallel to each other appear to approach or converge in the distance") — one principle, two applications. (3) XII is a miscellanea chapter ("Moon's Phases--Moon's appearance--Planet Neptune--Pendulum Experiments"), not a chapter assigned to the phases. (4) On the other side of the ledger, "a tilted Earth turning once a day while it goes round the Sun" is three independent stipulated inputs (rotation, obliquity, orbital revolution) counted as one. Under a symmetric count the six explananda cost the plane five and the globe three — still our way, but nothing like six against two. This is precisely the "metric wearing a lab coat" objection our own advocate block raises, and the sharpest version of it is available in the source text we quote elsewhere in the same entry, so a defender does not even have to leave our page to make it.
findings.fix: Rewrite the paragraph as a symmetric count and drop the number "six". Concede VI outright in one clause — "Rowbotham derives day and night and the seasons from IV and V himself: 'Thus, day and night, long and short days, Winter and Summer ... arise simply from the Sun's position in relation to the north pole' (Section 6) — so that one is his derivation, not his stipulation" — and then count what is genuinely stipulated on each side: on the plane, that the Sun circles daily over it (IV), that the circle's diameter varies annually with nothing to set it (V), that parallels converge at a finite vanishing point (VII, reused at XIII), a dark body for lunar eclipses (IX), and a phase mechanism for the Moon (XII); on the globe, daily rotation, axial tilt, and annual orbit, from which all six follow. Five against three, named on both sides. Then say what actually carries the weight, which is not the ratio: the plane still owes Section VIII, the southern sky, and the eclipse mechanism, and those are unpaid rather than merely numerous. In the TLDR, "gives sunrise, the seasons and the Sun's changing path a separate mechanism each" must go — in the source the seasons and the changing path are one mechanism; replace with "gives sunrise, the eclipses and the Sun's annually changing path a separate mechanism each, where a tilted Earth turning as it orbits delivers all of them from three."

findings.field: tldr, third sentence + refutation, fourth paragraph ("Fourth, the historical inversion") + sources[5] label
findings.problem: The historical-inversion headline — the entry's docstring calls it "THE HEADLINE" and says it is "DOCUMENTED IN TWO TRANSLATIONS" — rests on a construal that only one of the two translations supports, and we tell the reader they agree. The TLDR asserts flatly that "Ptolemy had already called the rotating-Earth account 'this simpler conjecture'", and the body says "Simpler is Ptolemy's word for his opponents' account, granted to them", offering Toomer as corroboration: "Toomer's independent rendering says the same thing." It does not say the same thing on the one word the claim needs. The unattributed CCSU text (Taliaferro's rendering) attaches the adjective to the hypothesis — "in accordance with this simpler conjecture"; Toomer, the standard scholarly translation and the one credited in MPRL footnote 32, attaches it to the mode of argument — "at least from simpler considerations", which reads as a concession about the level of analysis, not about the economy of the rival model. Both render the same Greek (kata ge to haplousteron), which is neuter and adverbial and genuinely bears Toomer's reading. So our own second citation, presented in the sources list as "an independent check on the wording", is the one that does not check the wording. A classicist or a well-informed defender will find this in one move, and it lands in the TLDR.
findings.fix: Stop claiming agreement on the operative word, and keep the part both renderings do support, which is all the argument needs. In the body: "Toomer, the standard modern translation, renders the same Greek differently where it matters — 'there is perhaps nothing in the celestial phenomena which would count against that hypothesis, at least from simpler considerations' — attaching 'simpler' to the level of argument rather than to the hypothesis. On either rendering the concession is the same and it is the concession that matters: Ptolemy grants the rotating Earth the appearances of the stars and rejects it on terrestrial physics, clouds and projectiles left behind by a turning Earth." In the TLDR, drop the direct attribution of the phrase to Ptolemy: "Ptolemy had already granted the rotating-Earth account the appearances of the stars and rejected it on terrestrial physics instead." And change the sources[5] label from "an independent check on the wording" to "the standard scholarly rendering, which differs from the CCSU text on where 'simpler' attaches".

findings.field: scripts/clusters.py D12 originator_work / year (reported up by this file, not applied)
findings.problem: The cluster record credits D12 to "Zetetic Astronomy", 1849, while the treatment quotes and cites WRK-ROWBOTHAM-1865 throughout, because the 16-page 1849 pamphlet was not reachable. The entry discloses this honestly in the gloss and does not publish a to-do, which is the right procedural move for a file that does not own clusters.py — so this is not a defect in the file under review. But it is the recurring failure the curmudgeon doc calls the highest-leverage one, and it has a live consequence here: build.py:144-145 and :162 push originator_work and originator_year into the published dataset, so 1849 is an unverified year sitting in data/ for a claim whose only located text is 1865. Under the project's own rule, an attribution that will not verify is withdrawn rather than left standing.
findings.fix: In scripts/clusters.py set D12 originator_work="Earth Not a Globe", year="1865", and anchor the edit on the cluster key "D12" — never on the originator= line, which is byte-identical across B02, B06, B07 and D12 and is exactly how the E01/E03 misfile was manufactured. Then rerun tests/run.sh, since the year distribution feeds published figures. If the operator would rather keep 1849 pending a copy of the pamphlet, the gloss sentence should say so explicitly rather than leaving the reader to reconcile two dates.

findings.problem: The advocate block misses the sharpest move available, and the miss is created by our own first paragraph. We open by conceding that parsimony's first legitimate job is to "break ties between rivals that predict the same observations" — which is precisely what the geocentric branch claims its position is, on general covariance (ARG-R01). A defender turns our sentence around: by our own statement of the rule, this is not an illegitimate use of parsimony at all, it is the licensed one, and the burden shifts to us to show the rivals are not empirically equivalent. The body does answer it, but only at the very end and implicitly (aberration, parallax, ring laser, barycentric correction), and the advocate block — which is where we are supposed to have found this first — does not raise it.
findings.fix: Add the move to advocate.best_defense in the defender's voice ("You concede parsimony breaks ties between rivals that predict the same observations. That is our claim about this case, so you have licensed the argument and then complained about it"), and close the door in the first paragraph of the refutation with one clause: "— and the tie-breaking job only arises once the rivals are shown to predict the same observations, which is the question aberration, parallax and the ring laser settle before parsimony is reached."

findings.problem: The TLDR opens "Simplicity is a preference, not a measurement" — which is the SURFACE bust the entry's own steelman labels "weak — do not use" and says "loses immediately", on the ground that parsimony is Newton's first Rule of Reasoning and is formalised in model selection "where the penalty on free parameters is derived rather than asserted". A reader who opens the steelman finds the page correcting its own summary, and a defender quotes our steelman against our TLDR. The body is right; the compression into a slogan is what fails.
findings.fix: Open the TLDR with the claim the body actually defends: "Simplicity is a real criterion, but it only decides anything once someone states a measure and counts under it, and no such count appears in either of the two summary chapters of Rowbotham searched here."

findings.problem: "he names the specimen rather than gesturing at one" overstates what Rowbotham does. He names the doctrine — "some other and 'central Sun' which has been assumed to be the true axis and centre of the Universe" — but he names neither Maedler nor the Pleiades anywhere in the passage. The identification of his target with Maedler's Central Sun hypothesis is ours, and the sentence as written invites the reader to think it is his.
findings.fix: "...and he names the doctrine rather than gesturing at a vague excess of motions — the identification with J. H. von Maedler's Central Sun hypothesis, which placed that centre in the Pleiades, is ours."

findings.problem: The paragraph that answers our own KERNEL ends: "The entrainment hypothesis got its altitude and its independent replication, and neither produced Miller's signal." The Joos half is sourced. The altitude half is not, and the source we cite for the move supplies no result: Swenson p. 225 records the summer-1930 installation in the base of the 100-inch and then goes straight to Joos, and his note 29 says the opposite of a clean outcome — correspondence of January 1930 "indicates that Michelson had lost interest by then and that the latest observational data was not suitable for publication." I could find no published result from the Mount Wilson installation. So our answer to the defender's strongest point asserts an experimental outcome we cannot cite, in a field whose whole job is to be unimpeachable. Miller's heir says in one line: the mountain data was never published, so you cannot quote it against me.
findings.fix: Rewrite the concession honestly: "Acted on: in the summer of 1930 Pease and Pearson had the instrument carried up the mountain and installed in the base of the 100-inch telescope — the elevation Miller asked for. No result from that installation is reported in Swenson's account, whose note records that by January 1930 Michelson had lost interest and that the latest data was 'not suitable for publication'. What answered the objection was Joos, who in the same season ran a 21-metre interferometer at Jena, in Miller's own direct response, and reported an effect 'less than 1/1000 of a fringe width ... less than 1.5 km/sec'." That is both true and stronger, because it concedes the loose end before a defender finds it.

findings.field: scripts/clusters.py A11 note (renders as the Refutation summary line inside this card, render.py:180)
findings.problem: The cluster note reads "A high-precision repeat of Michelson–Morley (expected 0.9 fringe, measured 0.01), run by Michelson at Mount Wilson specifically to test Miller." build.py:161 maps note -> basis and render.py:180 prints basis as the summary line of section 3, directly above a refutation whose section 2 is headed "The higher altitude did not happen" and states the site was Pasadena. Two of that sentence's three factual claims are wrong on our own evidence: the site was the observatory's Pasadena laboratory (Miller 1933 RMP 5:240; Swenson pp. 220-221; the comparison table's own location field, "Pasadena (Mt. Wilson optical shop)"), and Pease and Pearson did the observing under Michelson's supervision. A reader who never expands the card sees only the wrong version. The docstring (note 11b) reports this and does not fix it — the E01/E03 "recorded, not applied" pattern, on the one fact this entry is distinctive for.
findings.fix: Operator action, anchored on the cluster key "A11" and never on the originator= line: note="A high-precision repeat of Michelson–Morley (expected 0.9 fringe, measured 0.01), run by Pease and Pearson under Michelson at the Mount Wilson Observatory's Pasadena laboratory, specifically to test Miller. Same non-discriminating status as A01." While there, real_source should carry both printings — the sentence the whole downstream tradition quotes is the Nature note of 19 Jan 1929, and the two printings give different ratios.

findings.problem: The opening sentence asserts "the chain that carried it to this list turned that into a detection of 20 km/s". The body twice refuses that claim: the gloss says "the specimen carries no citation for item 10 ... so which text its compiler read is not something this page can show", the compression note repeats it, and verdict_challenge names it as the challenge's weak point ("we cannot show the compiler read this book rather than a textbook table that calls the result null"). The TLDR also sits oddly against its own third sentence — if the chain turned the null into a detection, the list would not be "the more orthodox party". This is the recurring failure: the summary claims a provenance the argument below it declines to claim, and the TLDR is escaped and rendered first, above everything that qualifies it.
findings.fix: Make the TLDR describe the tradition rather than a delivery path: "The 1929 experiment reported an upper limit ... and the geocentric literature this item is traced to turned that into a detection of 20 km/s by dividing 300 by 15, when a Michelson-Morley fringe shift goes as the square of the speed." One word ('literature' for 'chain that carried it to this list') removes a claim the page cannot support and costs the sentence nothing.

findings.problem: "the modern descendants are rotating optical cavities, which bound the anisotropy of the speed of light at Δc/c ≈ 10⁻¹⁷ (Herrmann et al. 2009) and 10⁻¹⁸ (Nagel et al. 2015) — fifteen orders of magnitude past 1929". The two bounds and both arXiv IDs are correct (1002.1284 = PRD 80:105011 2009; 1412.6954 = Nat. Commun. 6:8174 2015). The 'fifteen' is not. It appears to come from comparing the 1929 fringe-shift bound (0.01) with a fractional anisotropy (10⁻¹⁷) — different quantities. In the same units, 1929's v ≤ 3.1 km/s corresponds to Δc/c ~ (v/c)² ≈ 1×10⁻¹⁰, so the gain to 10⁻¹⁸ is about eight orders, not fifteen. A hostile reader checks exactly this kind of flourish, and eight orders is already overwhelming.
findings.fix: "...at Δc/c ≈ 10⁻¹⁷ and 10⁻¹⁸ — eight orders of magnitude past the 1929 bound, whose v ≤ 3 km/s corresponds to Δc/c of about 10⁻¹⁰ — still null, still exactly what relativity predicts for an Earth in motion."

findings.field: refutation, section 1, third paragraph (and passage.gloss, fourth paragraph)
findings.problem: We quote Swenson to establish the two-printing discrepancy and stop one clause short. His sentence (p. 222) reads in full: "Later, in March, the Journal of the Optical Society of America reported that nothing was observed within one-fiftieth of the expected shift, based on Sternberg's estimate of the solar system's resultant velocity of about three thousand kilometers per second." Our text cuts at 'expected shift'. The omitted clause is material to the arithmetic on the same page: the gloss prints Munera's 42.4 km/s for the JOSA figure, which is 300/√50 and presupposes the 300 km/s basis Swenson explicitly does not give it. So in the passage whose point is that the book prints three unreconciled velocities without noticing, we print a derived velocity our own cited historian contradicts, and we truncate him at the clause that would show it. Neither of the two 1929 printings was reached (the entry says so), so this is the only evidence we have on the question.
findings.fix: Restore the clause and turn it into a point: "...reported that nothing was observed within one-fiftieth of the expected shift — 'based on Sternberg's estimate of the solar system's resultant velocity of about three thousand kilometers per second', which is not the 300 km/s the Nature figure references, so Munera's 42.4 km/s for the JOSA printing rests on a basis Swenson's account does not support. Neither printing was reached for this entry; the ratios are as reported by Swenson and Munera." Also drop 'the record is clear' from the paragraph's opening — the record is documented, not clear.

findings.problem: "The book treats this experiment as a Michelson-Morley repetition about translation through the ether, and puts rotation elsewhere — in Michelson-Gale and Sagnac ... Nothing in its pages on Michelson-Pease-Pearson locates a rotation claim." Our own refutation section 5 quotes footnote 752 — "It is precisely the rotation of the ether every 24 hours that accounts for the small positive results of all the interferometer experiments at the surface of the Earth" — and that footnote sits at the foot of printed p. 387, i.e. inside the pages the note says contain no rotation claim, attached to the Michelson-Pease-Pearson discussion and expressly covering 'all the interferometer experiments'. Two published fields of the same entry contradict each other, and it happens in the compression block, which is the project's flagship finding field. It is also an absence claim scoped only to 'its pages on Michelson-Pease-Pearson' — no edition, no page range, no route — which is weaker than the rule asks even where it is true.
findings.fix: "No claim that this experiment measured the Earth's rotation is located in the archive.org OCR's pages on Michelson-Pease-Pearson (printed pp. 385–387) or at the 'null' mention on p. 353. Rotation does appear there, but as the book's explanation rather than as the experiment's subject: footnote 752, at the foot of p. 387, credits 'the rotation of the ether every 24 hours' with the small positive results of all the interferometer experiments — a mechanism answered on its own numbers in the refutation."

findings.field: refutation section 6, and the Wettzell entry in sources
findings.problem: "the ring laser at Wettzell ... tracks the Earth's rotation rate below one part in 10⁹ and resolves length-of-day variation and polar motion in agreement with very-long-baseline interferometry", cited to Eur. Phys. J. C 82 (2022), doi 10.1140/epjc/s10052-022-10798-9. That paper ('Overcoming 1 part in 10⁹ of earth angular rotation rate measurement with the G Wettzell data') supports the first half — its Allan deviation drops below 1 part in 10⁹ after about 10⁴ s of integration, on two three-day data sets. It does not support the second: it contains no mention of VLBI or of length-of-day, and it treats diurnal polar motion only as a modelled correction that is subtracted, adding that those corrections 'have to be considered as preliminary'. The underlying claim is true of the ring-laser literature; it is not true of this citation, and on a project whose product is provenance, a claim attached to a paper that does not make it is the worst available error.
findings.fix: Either narrow the sentence to what the paper says ('resolves the Earth's rotation rate below one part in 10⁹ after hours of integration') or add the citation that carries the rest — Schreiber et al. on direct ring-laser measurement of polar motion, cross-checked against the IERS/VLBI series — and split the source label accordingly.

findings.problem: "The main text at p. 386 divides: 'if one multiplies his three hundred kilometers per second by one-fifteenth, the result is 20 km/sec'." That sentence is on printed p. 387, not 386. In the archive.org OCR the folio is a running foot, so the leaf carrying it (leaf 399) ends '...755 Einstein: The Life and Times, p. 107. 387'. The entry's other page cites are all correct — p. 353, pp. 385-386 for the three attempts, p. 386 for Michelson's quoted paragraph and 'significant fringe shifting', p. 387 for the 'two ways' sentence — which makes this the only slip, and it is in published prose.
findings.fix: 'The main text at p. 387 divides: ...'

findings.problem: "where it does call the result null, the word is inside its own quotation marks" is a universal claim about the book with no scope on it. The gloss states the same thing correctly — 'The book uses the word "null" of this experiment once in the text reachable here' — and the compression note scopes it too ('the one place the reachable text applies the word'). The TLDR is what a reader meets first, and it is the one field of the three that asserts an absence unscoped. (I checked: within that OCR it is true — all nine occurrences of 'Pease' — but the reader has no way to know what was searched.)
findings.fix: "...where the text we could reach calls the result null, the word is inside the book's own quotation marks".

findings.field: sources (Munera entry; Sungenis Vol. I entry)
findings.problem: Two provenance labels overstate slightly. The Munera entry says he is 'quoted here only as it appears in Galileo Was Wrong Vol. I n. 689' — but straw_man quotes him from footnote 687 ('an inconsistency between observation (a non-zero velocity) and interpretation (a null result)'), which I verified at the foot of p. 352. The Sungenis entry says 'footnotes 689 and 751–759 at the feet of those pages'; 751-755 are at pp. 386-387, but 756-759 are at pp. 389-390, in the Galaev section. findings.fix: '...quoted here only as he appears in Galileo Was Wrong Vol. I, nn. 687 and 689'; and 'footnotes 689 (p. 353) and 751–755 (pp. 386–387); Galaev's 6,000 m/s at n. 759, p. 390'.

findings.problem: Section 2 says the light path 'went to 52 metres' (the book's round-trip figure) and section 4 computes with 'the 1928 path length of 25.9 m' (the one-way figure the standard table and Miller 1933's D = 2592 cm both give). Both are right and they are the same instrument, but the page never says so, and a reader who notices the factor of two has been handed an apparent contradiction inside the section that carries our arithmetic.
findings.fix: In section 4, one clause: 'With the 1928 one-way path of 25.9 m — the eighty-five feet Swenson records, quoted above as a 52-metre round trip — that is...'

findings.problem: "within a single British survey the predicted lean between stations is a matter of arcseconds and is swamped by exactly the local effects that produced Rowbotham's anomaly" is false, and it contradicts our own refutation. The table's stations are Dunnose (50 deg 37' 08") to Clifton (53 deg 27' 31"): the two verticals lean by 2.84 deg, about 10,200 arcseconds. Dunnose to Greenwich alone is 51' 32" = 3,092 arcseconds. That lean is not a small effect swamped by local ones; it IS the astronomical latitude difference the survey measured, and the 2-4" station deflections perturb it at the 0.2% level - which is exactly what refutation section 3 says two paragraphs earlier. As written, the block makes Rowbotham's inference look reasonable at British scale and hands a critic a self-contradiction inside one entry.
findings.fix: Replace with the true reason the widening matters: within the survey the lean between stations is degrees, and it is the very quantity Rowbotham's table records as latitude - his own evidence presupposes it. The item's "worldwide" then adds the scale at which two verticals differ by up to 180 degrees and bridge towers are built non-parallel on purpose. Do not describe the British-scale lean as arcseconds; that number belongs to the deflection of the vertical, not to the lean.

findings.problem: Sensors 16(4):565 (2016) is credited to "Barzaghi et al." The paper is real and the title, journal, volume, issue and year are all correct, but its authors are Luca Vittuari, Maria Alessandra Tini, Pierguido Sarti, Eugenio Serantoni, Alessandra Borghi, Monia Negusini and Sebastien Guillaume (verified at mdpi.com/1424-8220/16/4/565). Barzaghi is not among them; the slip is most likely from the ITALGEO geoid model the paper uses. A misattributed citation in a published source list is the worst available error on a site whose product is provenance.
findings.fix: Relabel as "Vittuari et al., 'A Comparative Study of the Applied Methods for Estimating Deflection of the Vertical in Terrestrial Geodetic Measurements', Sensors 16(4):565 (2016)".

findings.problem: "on its shortest arc, Dunnose to Greenwich at about 0.86 deg" - Dunnose-Greenwich is the second shortest arc in Rowbotham's table, not the shortest. Solving the table's own mean-latitude column gives Clifton 53 deg 27' 31", Greenwich 51 deg 28' 40", Arbury Hill 52 deg 13' 28", Dunnose 50 deg 37' 08" (each cross-checks against the published station latitudes). Arbury Hill-Greenwich is 44' 48" = 0.747 deg; Dunnose-Greenwich is 51' 32" = 0.859 deg. A defender who opens the table catches this in a minute, and the whole magnitude argument turns on picking the most sensitive arc.
findings.fix: Name Arbury Hill to Greenwich, 0.747 deg = 2,688 arcseconds, and recompute: 0.20% of that is 5.4 arcseconds of latitude error - still squarely inside the Britannica's range, and a stronger version of the same point.

findings.problem: Both quoted quantities from the Sensors paper are attached to the wrong referents. "The first two agree 'well within the 1 arcsec level'" - the paper's phrase describes the standard deviations of the GNSS-plus-levelling method alone ("The method that combines leveling and GNSS has slightly larger standard deviations; although well within the 1 arcsec level, which was assumed as threshold"), not the agreement between two methods. And "the gravity-derived values sit about 2.5 arcseconds out" turns a standard deviation into an offset: the paper says "the geoid model based method, whose 2.5 arcsec standard deviations exceed this threshold, is also statistically consistent with the others". The docstring gets this right; the prose does not.
findings.fix: Quote the sentence that actually supports the claim - "The three methods are in excellent agreement, with an operational supremacy of the astro-geodetic method" - and describe the 1 arcsec and 2.5 arcsec figures as each method's precision, with the geoid model "statistically consistent with the others" despite exceeding the 1 arcsec threshold.

findings.problem: The entry states as established history that the British arc anomaly was caused by deflection of the vertical: "traces to the plumb line being pulled sideways", "The explanation, when it came, was...", "its cause is the thing he was arguing against", "The arcs disagreed because...". The 1911 Britannica article we cite does not say this. It gives station deflections for the English survey and the "perplexity" remark, but its discussion of a prolate result is about the French Cassini arc, not the English one, and it presents the English survey as successful work. Our own docstring note 6 warns: "State this as a magnitude argument, NOT as a published reanalysis of that table - we did not find one." The published prose does the thing the note forbids, in four places including the TLDR.
findings.fix: Keep the magnitude argument and drop the causal verbs: the spread in his table is 0.20%, which on his most sensitive arc is about 5 arcseconds of latitude - the ordinary size of the station deflections the Britannica computed for that same survey. Say that no reanalysis of Rowbotham's specific table was located, so this is a consistency argument rather than a published attribution. In the TLDR, "is the size of" instead of "traces to".

findings.problem: Murray's "It has been found impossible to explain the want of agreement in a satisfactory way" is attached to the wrong discrepancy. In both the 1865 and 1881 texts that sentence refers to the mismatch between the polar/equatorial axis ratio derived from the Beachy Head-Dunnose degree perpendicular to the meridian and that from meridional degrees, and it comes BEFORE the table. The "oblong instead of an oblate spheroid" remark about the degrees decreasing comes after it. We present the concession as Murray admitting the table's northward decrease could not be explained ("his source concedes it could not be satisfactorily explained").
findings.fix: Attribute each remark to its own referent: Murray reports that the perpendicular-degree and meridional-degree results disagreed and that the disagreement could not be explained satisfactorily, AND separately that the tabulated degrees appear to decrease as if the Earth were oblong. Both are real, and keeping them apart costs one clause.

findings.problem: The advocate is rated 4, which the project's own rubric says must be answered in the body, and the fourth move - Tamarack, the only real side-by-side plumb-line experiment anyone can point at - is answered nowhere a reader can reach. render.py renders tldr, passage, steelman, refutation, compression, straw_man and verdict_challenge; it does not render advocate. So the preemptive's "That paragraph should be added to the body if this argument is ever attacked in public" parks the answer in an unpublished field, in the future tense. Refutation section 5 also asserts that neither text observed a plumb line, which invites the reader to ask whether anyone ever did.
findings.fix: Move the Tamarack arithmetic into the body as a short paragraph at the end of section 1 or 5: 15 ft of separation over 4,250 ft of depth predicts 0.0031 ft (about 0.9 mm) of convergence; McNair's results across the shafts ran -0.028 to +0.141 ft with error under 0.003 ft, so the apparatus could not have detected the effect in either direction - a statement about the shaft, not about the men. All of it is verified against Simanek's account (Science XV, 20 June 1902).

findings.problem: "the nautical mile IS one minute of latitude, 1,853 m". The international nautical mile has been defined as exactly 1,852 m since 1929, not as a minute of latitude; one minute of latitude itself runs from about 1,843 m at the equator to about 1,862 m at the poles. The historical origin is exactly as described, but the definition and the number as published are both wrong, and this sits in the paragraph doing the most rhetorical work.
findings.fix: "the nautical mile was defined as one minute of latitude and is now fixed at exactly 1,852 m - the distance over which the plumb line turns by one arcminute relative to the sky".

findings.problem: The block attributes to the source a claim it does not make and that our own gloss shows it does not make. We write that the book's 'implicitly denied' remark 'misdescribes the state of the physics' because 'the alternative is not denied in the literature; it is computed in it.' But (a) the book's subject is the geokinetic argument, not the physics literature — its sentence is 'All the various effects noted above depend on the assumption that the inertial effects can only be caused by the Earth's rotation', which is a charge against the popular argument that our own refutation concedes in its opening paragraph; (b) on that same page the book itself cites the computation, 'Barbour and Bertotti proved that a large hollow sphere (representing the distant star fields) rotating around a small solid sphere inside ... produced exactly the same pattern of Coriolis and centrifugal forces', and the 2013 Vol. II contents list sections titled 'Brill and Cohen's Geocentrism', 'Lynden-Bell's Geocentrism' and 'Barbour and Bertotti's Geocentrism'; and (c) our own gloss four paragraphs earlier quotes Eddington denying exactly that alternative from inside the literature ('We do not believe that if the heavenly bodies were all annihilated it would upset the gyrocompass'). So the sentence is contradicted by the source, by the source's own bibliography, and by our own entry.
findings.fix: Drop 'That misdescribes the state of the physics. The alternative is not denied in the literature; it is computed in it.' Keep the part that survives and is the real point: the book cites the rotating-shell literature accurately, so what a stationary-Earth cosmology owes is not an acknowledgement that the equivalence exists but a dynamics for the rotating cosmos (ARG-R01). If a straw man is still to be identified here, identify the narrower one — that the response treats the Machian alternative as one the geokinetic side ignores, when Eddington's objection quoted in the book's own footnote 615 shows it was considered and rejected on grounds the book does not answer at this point.

findings.field: refutation, section 2 ('Two numbers, and they are the argument')
findings.problem: 'They are the two components of a single vector of fixed length, so sin²φ + cos²φ = 1 and their quadrature sum is the same 15.041° per hour at every latitude on Earth' does not follow from the two rates as displayed two paragraphs above, because the tilt rate carries a sin(azimuth) factor. sqrt((15 sinφ)² + (15 cosφ sin Az)²) = 15 only when |sin Az| = 1. For a gyro whose axis points north (Az = 0) the tilt rate is zero and the quadrature sum is 15 sinφ. The underlying vector claim is correct — the vertical and horizontal components of Ω are Ω sinφ and Ω cosφ and those do sum in quadrature to Ω — but the sentence identifies the horizontal component with the tilt rate, which is the component resolved against the rotor's own axis. advocate.preemptive (2) makes this the load the whole answer to the ether-vortex objection rests on, so it needs to be exactly right.
findings.fix: Say it about the field rather than the readings: 'The vertical and horizontal components of Ω are Ω sin φ and Ω cos φ, and those two sum in quadrature to the same 15.041°/hr everywhere. The drift rate reads the first directly; the tilt rate reads the second, reduced by sin (azimuth) because only the part of the horizontal component perpendicular to the rotor axis can torque it — set the axis east-west and the tilt rate is the horizontal component itself.'

findings.problem: The central theorem silently equates 'the local vertical' with the geometric normal to the plane. What a gyrocompass's pendulous mass or mercury ballistic actually responds to is apparent gravity — the plumb line. On a flat-earth model that keeps 'down' perpendicular to the plane, the two coincide and the theorem is airtight; on a model with a self-gravitating disc the plumb line tilts inward with radius and the angle to a fixed rotation axis does vary from place to place. The entry's advocate section anticipates the ether-vortex escape but not this one, and it is the escape a physically literate defender reaches for.
findings.fix: Name the assumption and close it in a sentence: the theorem is about the direction the plumb line points, which on any flat model where 'down' is perpendicular to the plane is one direction everywhere; a model in which the plumb line tilts with distance from the centre has bought curvature under another name — a surface whose apparent vertical swings through a right angle is a curved equipotential, its ocean surface follows that equipotential, and it still cannot reverse the Foucault sense across a boundary it does not have.

findings.problem: The side-by-side blockquote a reader judges the drift from carries only the hedged material (p. 710 statement of the opposing case, p. 712 'has not been disproven experimentally'), and the note's argument — 'A not-disproven is not a result' — reads as though the book stopped there. It did not: at p. 746 it states flatly that the free motion of the pendulum and of the Michelson-Gale ring define planes 'relative to the rotating heavens'. Our own gloss prints that sentence and says so. Quoting a source up to the disjunction in the very field built to display the drift is the hedge rule violated on our side, and it makes the drift look larger than the evidence shows.
findings.fix: Add the p. 746 sentence to source_wording, then state why force_upgraded survives it: the book's flat statement is about FREE instruments — a pendulum and a light ring — while item 229 asserts it of the gyrocompass, the one instrument built to be Earth-referenced. That is the drift, and it is stronger with the flat statement in view than without it.

findings.problem: One of the two surviving legs of the self-contradiction is asserted rather than defended, and the entry's own concession is the tool that removes it. Item 224 is four words — 'No rotation proof mechanical.' — and in the geocentric idiom it reads 'there is no mechanical proof that the EARTH rotates', which is exactly what the refutation's first paragraph concedes ('no gyroscopic instrument can tell you whether the Earth turns or the cosmos turns around it') and what section 7 repeats. On that reading 224 is consistent with 229, not a denial of it, and the contradiction rests on item 12 alone. The entry answers a different objection (instrument grade) and then asserts 'it is a straight disagreement about whether there is a daily relative rotation for a gyroscope to register at all' without showing that the four words force that reading.
findings.fix: Either drop 224 and rest the verdict on item 12, whose 'anomalies indicating no rotation' is a reading-level claim already shown reversed by the originator's own filmed 15°/hr at ARG-A07 — or keep 224 and disarm the escape explicitly: 'Read 224 as no proof that the Earth in particular turns and it is not a contradiction, it is this page's own concession — in which case the list has published as proof a claim its own item 229 renders non-discriminating. Read it as no mechanical rotation detected at all and it contradicts 229. The list gives no way to tell which, and neither reading leaves item 229 standing.'

findings.problem: 'the item has named the one gyroscopic instrument in the world that is engineered not to be sky-locked' is a uniqueness claim that fails. A gyrotheodolite (mine and tunnel surveying) is a north-seeking gyro built on the same principle, and gyro-stabilised INS platforms are continuously torqued to stay locally level and north-referenced. The TLDR inherits the claim as 'the instrument built to break exactly that'.
findings.fix: 'the item has named the class of gyroscopic instrument engineered not to be sky-locked'. Then take the gain: a gyrotheodolite's north-seeking accuracy degrades as cos φ exactly as a marine gyrocompass does, on land, with no shipping industry involved — which is a direct answer to the advocate's fourth move that the entry currently has no reply to.

findings.problem: 'the third of three "geokinetic claims" it lists at p. 709 before answering them' misdescribes the structure of the page it quotes. On the actual p. 710 the book's three geokinetic claims are (1) spin, (2) heliocentric, (3) cosmic linear. The Sagnac/gyrocompass sentence is the third item in a different, later list, under the heading 'The Geokinetic Claim' in Part 1, enumerating the inertial-force effects offered for the spin claim. The substance of our point — the book is stating the other side's case in order to answer it — is correct.
findings.fix: 'the third of three inertial-force effects the book lists at p. 710 under "The Geokinetic Claim", the case for the daily spin as it sets it out before answering it'.

Full treatment for ARG-B11 written to /home/claude/spinning-ball-review/scripts/_b10_B11.py (570 lines): long research docstring, then ENTRY = {"B11": dict(...)} with tldr, passage=None + untraceable, steelman, refutation, advocate (survives=4), straw_man, compression, verdict_challenge, people, related, and 21 sources.

PROVENANCE — untraced, and the search terminated in a result. Searched offline 2026-08-10: Galileo Was Wrong Vol. I (462,032 words) and Vol. II (284,044 words) full text — photogrammetry, sonar, bathymetry, LiDAR, synthetic aperture, echo sounding not located in either as searched; all 46 "radar" occurrences read individually and every one is the Shapiro/Wallace Venus time-delay material, Van Flandern's planetary radar-ranging item, the one DoD/GPS sentence, a contents or bibliography line, or (once) the metaphor "a blip on the radar screen". Dubay's 200 Proofs: zero for every term. TFES wiki FAQ: none located. FlatEarth.ws catalogues exactly one flat-earth radar claim and it is a different one (marine radar advertised ranges), with no originator named. Rowbotham/Carpenter deliberately not searched — the instruments postdate them; pre_modern considered and rejected for the same reason. The finding that replaces an ancestor: items 385–402 are eighteen consecutive lines, one per profession, mostly without verbs — a list grown by enumerating disciplines rather than by citing anyone.

KERNEL (conceded at full strength before anything is answered): all four disciplines contain a real, named, daily-used flat-Earth object — plane earth loss in RF propagation, Cartesian collinearity equations in photogrammetry, "flat earth phase removal" in InSAR, the isovelocity assumption in shallow-water acoustics. The surface bust loses to a citation and the entry says so. It doesn't save the claim because each field also publishes the LIMIT, and the limit is computed from R — cleanest statement being Yang et al., IEEE Trans. Veh. The hedge-rule finding is the entry. The easy rebuttal - "dip is measurable with a theodolite" - is the one our own cluster note carries, and Rowbotham answered it in 1881. THE "DIP SECTOR" (3rd ed., p. 235) scopes the claim: "unless some telescopic instrument is used no dip whatever is required to meet the sea horizon." Under THEODOLITE TANGENT he concedes the measurement outright: "The author has made experiments similar to the above, and found it to be as stated; but the cause is not that the line of sight is a tangent, but the same 'collimation'." So the real claim is that the dip is an artefact of the telescope, and that is what the refutation answers.

Kernel, three discriminators none of which needs a photograph from orbit: collimation error reverses sign under face-left/face-right and the dip does not; collimation is a constant of the instrument and cannot scale as sqrt(h); and the same single cause is offered for spherical excess, which grows as A/R^2 (recomputed: 1.98"/7.92"/22.0" for 30/60/100 km equilateral triangles) while Rowbotham's own block quotation states that the excess is "inappreciable in common cases, but in the larger triangles it becomes necessary to allow for it".

The sharpest new finding is arithmetic. For a balloon two miles up Rowbotham computes the horizon at "127 miles away" and "over 20,000 feet below the line of sight" - both correct (sphere: 125.8 miles, 2h = 21,120 ft) - and concludes the dip "would be so great that the aeronaut could not fail to observe it". arctan(21,120 ft / 125.8 mi) = 1.82 degrees. The ratio is not taken anywhere in the section. Same shape at Experiment 11 (Brighton pier, 34 ft, his own "68 feet": 6.2 arcminutes).

Straw man is theirs, twice: Carpenter proof 30 sources its "ten to nearly fifty degrees" to "astronomical diagrams" (those dips need altitudes of 98 km and 3,540 km); and Rowbotham's Experiment 7 / Dubay proof 60 both predict that on a globe the horizon would "decline towards the extremities" of a levelled board - a sphere's horizon is a circle at CONSTANT angular depression in every azimuth, so the sphere predicts a uniform offset and no decline, which is what they observe and report as proof of a plane.

The source states the gyrocompass claim as the OPPOSING side's case and answers it with Mach's principle and an explicit "it has not been disproven experimentally"; the refutation therefore concedes, in its first paragraph and in bold, both that a free gyroscope is genuinely sky-locked and that no gyroscopic instrument can say whether the Earth or the cosmos turns. Per the hedge rule's second clause it does not stop at that disjunction: the book states flatly at p. 745 that the heavens rotate, and the entry answers that. The refutation then moves where Mach cannot follow — from rotation to shape. A gyrocompass's directive force goes as cos(latitude) and its free-gyro drift as sin(latitude): two components of one vector in quadrature, varying only because the local vertical swings 90 degrees between equator and pole. On a plane the local vertical is one direction everywhere, so no gyroscopic quantity can vary with position, whatever rotates.
